subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, January 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. H. Jorgenson for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Argue.
The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At the
hour of adjournment on Friday, Mr. Speaker, I had commented with regard to the so-called march on Ottawa. I should like to comment on that a little further by issuing a personal warning to the officers of the farm union in western Canada to be very careful about becoming entangled in this march, because it is becoming political in nature. I say that because in the last two years when the farm unions of western Canada have come to Ottawa they have been well received by this government, in marked contrast to the manner in which they had been received by previous governments. I would think that it would be extremely dangerous for them to upset the confidence which they have already gained.
To comment further with regard to the agricultural situation I should like to say something with regard to the production of hogs. We all know that we are facing a pork surplus. I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture-and I hope he will give the matter consideration-that if there is necessity to lower the pork floor price, it should not be done but rather that commercial producers be excluded from that floor price. In other words I suggest that the support be made available to bona fide farmers only. I think this will do more than anything else to preserve our small farmers and family farms and to prevent vertical integration.
I should now like to make a few remarks with regard to the employment situation. First of all I should like to commend the Minister of Labour and the other members of the cabinet. Because of their actions and the actions of this government I can report to the house that unemployment in my constituency is at a minimum. It is less this winter than it has been in previous winters under the Liberal regime. This situation is a direct result of the action of this government, particularly with regard to housing. This has put to work this winter many hundreds of our loggers who would not otherwise have been employed, together with the action of the Minister of Labour in instituting the municipal work program. As you may have realized, Mr. Speaker, the province of Alberta is a leading province in taking advantage of this program. I should like to say to the minister that this program is working out very well. I can say to him that he has put hundreds of men to work in my constituency alone.
I also commend the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources for the work program in Jasper park. It is getting some
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1
vitally needed work done. It is not a relief program; it is a program for the development of our resources.
With regard to some of the speeches which have been made in this house by members of the opposition, I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Edmonton Journal in the early part of November. It is entitled "Playing Politics with Misery". The first paragraph of that editorial gives some figures which are not now relevant, but it goes on to state as follows:
The jobless totals include many unemployables, farmers and farmers' sons who register for other jobs as soon as harvest work is completed, persons changing jobs of their own volition, and so on.
While farm employment was down, employment in several other lines was higher. Non-farm employment was virtually at the same level as last year although, of course, Canada's working population is greater. On the prairies, persons with jobs totalled 1,641,000 which was 17,000 more than lest year but 6,000 fewer than September. Nevertheless, the picture of a substantial number of Canadians able and willing to work and unable to find jobs is not one to gloss over.
What must be deplored is the eagerness in certain quarters to play politics with the misfortune of thousands of feliow-Canadians. Stanley Knowles, executive vice-president of the Canadian Labour Congress and former C.C.F. member for parliament, was swift to demand that Prime Minister Diefenbaker break off his world tour and rush home to deal with the unemployment situation. Liberal Leader Pearson's position was little more creditable when he tried to create the impression that government policies are responsible for the unemployment total. He knows perfectly well that such is not the case.
Mr. Diefenbaker can do much more good by seeking markets for Canadian products abroad than by rushing home and calling a special session of parliament. However, his efforts and the efforts of everyone else in promoting trade will be worthless if industry and labour continue on their merry way pursuing policies that price our goods out of the world market and stoke the fires of inflation at home.
Socialists who never overlook a chance to exploit dislocations in the economy have a private motive. Their burning ambition is to destroy our free enterprise system. Those who are deceived thereby should know that if free enterprise is destroyed everything else free, including personal liberty, will be destroyed with it. Inflation does not disturb a socialist; he sees it as a means to hasten the overthrow of our system.
I think that editorial neatly sums up some of the speeches we have heard in this house regarding unemployment and the situation in Canada. We do need to have more insight shown by our labour union leaders, and, probably one of the reasons they have not time to show this insight is that they are becoming involved in politics and because they, like the farmers union leaders, can no longer speak for the rank and file. That is the important thing they should be considering at this time.
We do not only have to consider labour when we are asking ourselves how well a

job is done, but management also. We have too many large corporations whose management is topheavy. We ask labour to increase production when they want a raise in wages; we must also ask management to increase production before they receive an increase from investment. Indeed, if they are to maintain the benefits which they now receive they must show this country that they can produce more at less cost and with smaller executive power.
We have heard a great deal with regard to inflation. Inflation is not something which began last year or the year before. It has been going on for a long time, since even before the second world war. I think the basic explanation of inflation is that the cost of goods or services is above their actual value. As I say, this is nothing new; it has been going on for years, and one of the major causes of inflation, and particularly of its rapid increase over the past ten or twelve years, has been the extravagance and misspending of the former government. We in western Canada do not need to look at the printing bureau. We have our own printing bureaux in every one of our western constituencies. I have one in particular in Jasper park, where buildings were erected at fantastic prices and where roads were built at fantastic prices, roads which failed to stand up for even a limited period of years.
There is nothing wrong about government spending to create employment, and this will not cause inflation as long as we are diligent to ensure that value is received in return for this expenditure. This requires leadership, and I am sure the whole country agrees we now have that leadership under the present government.
I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the operation of the Canadian National Railways, because they are the vital link in my constituency. Here I point the finger at management, and at the failure of the management of the C.N.R. to use some imagination and initiative in order to establish that railway as a proper competitor of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When we talk about freight rates, rates upon which the whole of our economy in western Canada is based, this is the first thing we think of; and we ask ourselves, can management improve its competitive position? We think it could. We think more could and should be done by management to bring our freight rates into line. I think it is an admission of failure on the part of management when every time costs go up, they immediately go to the board of transport commissioners asking for an increase in freight rates. I know that some of the railroads in the United States made money during the past year and are now 66968-9-20
The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner paying 4 per cent to their shareholders. We in western Canada were, of course, very happy at the assurance by the Prime Minister that the Crownsnest pass rates will not be altered. We depend on them for our livelihood.
Now I should like to make a few remarks on the oil and gas industry. If I may I should just like to note the very inaccurate statement made by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) in this connection speaking in the debate last Wednesday, as recorded at page 166 of Hansard of January 21. The hon. member said:
Hon. members will also recall that about the same time, or shortly afterwards, the United States accommodated the Prime Minister by cutting off 15 per cent of our oil imports into the northwestern United States.
Mr. Speaker, that speech indicated that the Liberal party knows absolutely nothing about the oil industry in western Canada. We have heard that before in western Canada. Our friends in the Liberal party walked up and down our constituencies that produced the oil and said, "this government has now cut off 15 per cent of your exports," and so on.
This was not true. This is obviously inaccurate, for the simple reason that the exportation of oil into the United States does not depend on any government action but rather depends on available markets. We have today a world oil surplus. We have not been able to export to the United States even the amount of our allowable quota of oil, and never have we been able to do this. The hon. gentleman was completely wrong when he said there was any discrimination on the part of the Prime Minister or this government with respect to the exportation of oil.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal party is now so dead that it does not have the imagination or scope to know how big the oil industry is in western Canada or how much it can do for this country. I should like to cite a few figures concerning last year's oil operations in Alberta during a period of recession and in the face of a world oil surplus. The oil industry has confidence in the leadership of this government. To prove this I need only mention that those involved in the industry went ahead with exploration and the drilling of new wells. While our oil production was down 13 per cent last year our oil well completions were up. Total drilling footage was down 11 per cent but our total exploration expenses were up 7 per cent. For the education of hon. members opposite I should like to state that if a market for Canadian oil could be found we could wipe out our entire trade deficit with
298	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner the United States in one fell swoop. That is an indication of how big the industry is, and it is just starting.
The oil wells in my constituency produce well over 35 per cent of all the oil produced in Alberta, and new fields are now being developed. One of the largest gas wells in the world is located there from drilling which has recently taken place on the Little Berland river. The new areas known as Swan Hills and Virginia Hills are the hottest finds in western Canada. These are situated right at the top of my constituency. All these things will require imagination and initiative in enacting legislation that will enable the oil industry to develop. This is one of the major industries in Canada and one of the most significant developments in our economy.
At the extreme western end of my constituency, of course, there is Jasper national park. I wish to say a few words in this regard, because the change in government has meant a great change for the people living in this park. For the first time in history the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) visited the park, sat down with the people there and discussed with them their problems. That was never done before. The former minister under the old regime came out to Jasper but would not talk to the people there. He said he was not interested in the people but was worried about the bears.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is ridiculous.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources for his attitude and the interest he expressed in the problems of those living in this park, because they do have problems. I should also like to remind him of the promise he made to establish a commission to study the question of municipal government in the national parks town sites in western Canada with a view to solving many of the problems presently confronting the people in those areas.
We cannot talk about Jasper national park without talking about the Yellowhead highway. We are very happy that in the near future, within three or four years, we will have a highway running through Jasper. I hope arrangements can be made with the government of British Columbia so the route from Kamloops to Yellowhead may be completed.
Before taking my seat I wish to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McPhillips) to the effect that the old age pension should be extended to old age pensioners living outside Canada. This is fair and just, in my opinion, and I trust the government will give this matter sympathetic consideration.


In conclusion may I say that we in Canada are on the verge of a great development. We need in this country the leadership of our Prime Minister. There is no room in Canada, in view of its challenging and progressive future, for speeches such as have been made by some hon. members of the opposition. We need imagination and initiative and young people who will develop our northland. Opportunities have never before existed in Canada to the extent that they now exist in our northwest, and they should constitute a compelling challenge to young Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I should not like to begin my remarks without extending the conventional-and perhaps a little bit more than the conventional

compliments to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It perhaps will not surprise anyone in the house if I address my observations first to the seconder, because I think all of us were curious to see what kind of person would succeed in the historic constituency of Montmagny-L'Islet the most promising Canadian of his race who has come into this house since the war, a man who is now giving to his province the kind of leadership many of us feel it has needed for a long time.
I think the hon. member who now has the honour to represent this constituency acquitted himself with distinction. I believe, too, we can say that he expressed the kind of sentiments one would have expected to hear expressed by the successor of Mr. Lesage.

speechtext:
But the hon. member for Provencher is a veteran of two parliaments. When I read in the newspapers that he was to be given the honour of moving the address this year I confess that I thought this was another example of the confusion of the

Rather than to lose votes in the June 10 election, the Liberal government preferred to maintain its tight money policy, a policy that was driving small manufacturers and small businessmen to bankruptcy. Well, Mr. Speaker, under the leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), we did not rest on our laurels. On the contrary, we faced the problem squarely, and took action where the urgency was greatest.
The first step was to revive the confidence of the Canadian people, because business had slowed down. Industrial construction had begun to slacken, and feelings of "recession", mainly of a psychological nature, were in evidence, as the people had lost confidence in the economic future of the country.
The Address-Mr. Balcer
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the first task was to restore people's confidence and this we decided to do by circulating more money. It was a matter of putting money into the people's hands.
The situation was the more difficult as a similar recession was also beginning to make itself felt in the United States. Now we know that by and large the Canadian economy is geared to that of the United States. Well, without waiting to see what they would do, the government, under the present Prime Minister, took the lead and through various measures decided to put money into the hands of the public.
The first social measure which we tackled was that of old age security. Admittedly, this was relatively easy because, under the former government, old age pensions had remained so long at $40 a month that anyone who had at all considered the problem, could realize that the situation called for immediate improvement. That is why we raised those pensions from $46 to $55 a month, always in order to put a little money in the pockets of those Canadian citizens, to restore their selfrespect and provide them with the bare minimum to face their obligations.
Later on, to relieve the economic squeeze crushing the people of Canada as a result of the former government's fiscal policy, we decided to cut taxes. We did cut them to the extent of $189 million, while the Liberals, barely a few months before, and in spite of the predictions made to them by their economists, preferred to keep on taxing to the utmost the Canadian people and thus accumulate surpluses.
Of course, at the previous session, the Liberal government had cut certain taxes, but always on some insignificant items, such as chewing gum.
Mr. Speaker, when we decided to cut taxes, we did so having in mind primarily low wage earners and large families. In this way we have made available to the public an amount of $189 million which was actually needed.
We also launched a vast construction program. As everybody knows, construction is one way to deal directly or indirectly, with recession and unemployment. Well, we gave Canada the strongest home building policy it ever had. We gave impetus to lagging construction. We made $750 million available to builders and breadwinners. We improved legislation to make it easier for home builders and owners to borrow and repay.

The Address-Mr. Balcer
Well, let us take a look at the results of this splendid policy. In 1957, 122,340 dwelling units were started whereas in 1958, not in the full year, but only during the first eleven months, there were 155,036 starts; as to housing completions, there were 117,283 in 1957 but 133,217 in the first eleven months of
1958.	This is an all-time record in the history of this country. Through these efforts, huge sums were put at the disposal of the Canadian people, so that now in January
1959,	we are beginning to see a decrease of unemployment and we can look forward to an early solution to this problem.
And all along, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) was extending unemployment insurance benefits and was launching a winter works project. This campaign launched throughout Canada has already started to give results and everywhere, in spite of our harsh winters, like this year when the temperature is often below zero and people in all parts of Canada have put up with heavy storms, we see that in cities, large or small, construction is in full swing, people are improving the inside of their homes, putting in basements, or partitions, or new roofs, etc.
Well, as a result of a campaign sponsored by the Department of Labour, it was found that construction is no more expensive in winter, and perhaps less so than in summer. This is why builders and contractors have now decided to build during the winter, to the benefit of all concerned.
We took the necessary steps. First we upped security payments, we reduced taxes and finally we made several hundred million dollars available for construction, not to mention our public works program, the largest ever undertaken in this country. We went ahead with these measures before our neighbours to the south had made up their minds to do anything about them. Right after we had adopted these measures, the American press came up with similar proposals; but we were the ones who had taken the lead. Of course, in the meantime, our hon. friends opposite were saying that it was not enough, that our legislation was coming too late, that it was not adequate, and so on.
Well, the Prime Minister decided to ask the people what they thought about it. As we all know, whenever, in the past, a general election was held under the Liberal administration, it was always held at the most favourable time of the year, when either the crops, employment or trade were at high levels. In the past, an election was always called either in June or in August, always
[Mr. Balcer.l
at a time when, according to past experience, unemployment was at its lowest level or the harvest in full swing.
Well, when faced with the criticism of our hon. friends opposite, the Prime Minister of Canada did not wait for the best time of the year as regards employment-he could have waited till June, July or even August, because, as we recall, during the winter session of 1958, the Liberals were not particularly anxious to face the people once again. After planning all the program I have outlined earlier, our Prime Minister decided to face the nation again and to ask the people whether they accepted our party, which had fulfilled its promises. Furthermore, he asked the population to support the great program that had been launched on June 21. That is why he made his decision right in the middle of winter, when seasonal unemployment was at its peak and just when Canada was experiencing a wave of unemployment such as it had never seen before. Well, the people showed its confidence in the government and the government has not failed them.
The government carried on its work. It has always endeavoured to restore confidence among the people. That is why at the present time our foreign trade, just like our domestic and retail trade are reaching an all-time high so that we can look forward to increased prosperity in the coming months.
The construction program is going ahead, and, as mentioned in the speech from the throne, it is the intention of the government to speed up this program by making additional hundreds of millions available to the public, to provide jobs for the people of Canada.
And since we are on the subject of housing, I believe the people of Canada are confident that under the present government, this upsurge in house building will continue. Besides, economists agree on that necessity, since, as we know, children born in the early war years-and, at that time, Canada had the highest birth rate in its history-will, in the course of the next three, four, five or six years, reach the age when they will want to settle down. They will require houses and so, we can expect this gigantic building effort in Canada to extend into the next five or ten years. Another encouraging feature, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that not only is house building on the increase but industrial building also, which, as we know

had so significantly decreased, to the detriment of our economy, that this decrease can be considered as one of the great factors of this recession.
Well, we are happy to note, right now, in this very month of January, that in 1959, industrial building in Canada will expand as never before.
Let us take a look, for instance, at the picture in my own province of Quebec. In a single area of the province, the British Aluminum Company will spend $175 million the Quebec North Shore will spend $100 million while the Cartier Mining will spend $250 million and the Quebec Hydro $42 million. In addition, grain elevators, to be built in Baie Comeau, will involve an expenditure of $18 million. And, Mr. Speaker, this applies to only one area of the province, the newest, the Ungava area. This industrial construction is no doubt a harbinger of a well-balanced prosperity in this country.

Those, Mr. Speaker, are examples of the industrial upswing which is in evidence and which is anticipated in the spring of 1959. That is why I say that our hon. friends opposite have no reason to display such gloom, to worry as they do, because evidence of bright outlook can be seen throughout the country.
We also plan to expand the help being given to both home and industrial construction, and we propose to continue bringing before the house legislation which will be of greatest possible benefit to the Canadian people.
I am convinced that under the leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister, Canada faces an era of prosperity such as it has never known in all its history.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in this debate, and if I have to criticize the government as it deserves I intend that my remarks shall be as constructive as possible.
I should like first to pay tribute to you, Mr. Speaker, and tell you how we appreciate the manner in which you preside over the proceedings of this house. I should like also to convey our gratitude to the Deputy Speaker of this house (Mr. Sevigny). We congratulate him on his sense of justice and his kindness to the hon. members when he occupies the chair in your absence.
We are glad, also, to see that the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea) has been re-elected as deputy chairman of committees of the whole; we want to give him the assurance that we will always gladly co-operate with him.
Mr. Speaker, I want to join all those who spoke before me to offer my sincere congratulations to the movers of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Messrs. Jorgenson and Fortin).
The hon. member for Provencher has launched the debate very well, and the member for Montmagny-L'Islet has amazed us by his maiden speech here. His friends from Quebec should note his stand and try to imitate him on many of the points he mentioned which are, in brief, the fundamentals of the Liberal policy in this house and in the whole country.
Last Monday, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) made a remarkable speech. According to press comments and public

reaction, we see that he was quite right when he said that the government had shown almost a kind of genius in straying from the straight line to plunge into confusion, contradiction and wavering instability. The Leader of the Opposition was quite right also to say, last Monday, that the speech from the throne was more understandable for what it leaves out than for what it contains.
In my opinion, it is no exaggeration to say that the government, in outlining its legislative program for this session, has failed woefully by leaving out, and disregarding the three problems it was supposed to look into and which are of greatest concern to the Canadian people; unemployment, inflation, national defence, more particularly, air defence. Mr. Speaker, I shall not dwell on the latter subject. Our leader talked about it with authority. He stated the position of our party when he said that it is essential that we should be informed of all the aspects of the problem, either by parliamentary committee or by a sub-committee on estimates.
The Leader of the Opposition was right when he said last Monday that we have come to the crossroads in the field of defence and that, if we want to find a solution, we must give to this problem the best and most exhaustive consideration, since it is a matter of vital importance to the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we now face the problem of inflation and it is the responsibility of the government to take the necessary steps to stop the depreciation of our dollar, the rising cost of living and rising prices in all fields. Once again, the Leader of the Opposition had reason to criticize the government's failure to take action. We find nothing or, at least, very little, in the speech from the throne that could lead us to believe that the government intends to take the necessary and vigorous measures that will stop inflation. Inflation is detrimental to everybody. It is the main handicap to our country's economic development.
Increased costs of production are just about the most challenging problem at the present time, since Canadian producers are hardly able to meet foreign competition on world markets, indeed on the domestic market.
Of course, the responsibility for this does not lie at the door of the central government only. Provincial governments will also have

to reduce their expenditures, private enterprise will have to co-operate to a larger extent and all Canadians will have to do their share in helping to step up production. Even though this problem is not the sole responsibility of the federal government, it remains with them to take the lead and to implement the measures which are imperative.
At the annual general meeting of the Banque Canadienne Nationale, the president, Mr. St. Pierre, said at the end of his remarks on price inflation:
It is therefore imperative to resort forthwith to all possible means to control the erosion of currency which is threatening the welfare of our people and the future of Canada. It is the duty of the government to insure monetary stability through an adequate policy, and the first step in that direction is the elimination of the budgetary deficit.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to a problem which, in my opinion, is the most serious one at the present time, a problem which the Canadian people must face and which, in the words of His Eminence Cardinal Leger, is having many far-reaching consequences, and which the government must strive to solve: unemployment. It came to me as a surprise, Mr. Speaker, that the government hardly mentioned it in the speech from the throne. What is still more astonishing, is the fact that when a member on this side of the house deals with the problem, our hon. friends opposite get angry, charge us with spreading fear in the hearts of the Canadian people and with being unco-operative. They even go so far as to say that even though they have been responsible for managing the affairs of Canada for the past 18 months, the remarkable thing is that it behooves us, the opposition, to find the required solutions and to hand those solutions and suggestions over to them on a silver tray.
Mr. Speaker, there has been unemployment in the past and there will probably be some in the future. In the past, however, when there was unemployment, members who were then in the opposition did not fail to level harsh criticism at the government whose responsibility it was to remedy the situation. Now the shoe is on the other foot, with this difference that, during the years we were in power, we took all steps called for by existing conditions. As far as I am concerned, our honourable friends' tantrums leave me cold; moreover I am going to say that I quite intend to keep pleading in favour of my distressed fellow citizens.
The Address-Mr. Dumas
Some areas of Canada are more affected than others, nevertheless unemployment today is too widespread.
For example in my constituency there are too many workers who are out of a job. And what is more serious is the fact that in my riding as well as elsewhere, workers who have run out of regular and seasonal benefits find themselves in an unbearable predicament. In addition, those who get a temporary job but who will not be in a position to keep that job long enough to be entitled to benefits are in the same boat, and it is then that the situation becomes serious.
Mr. Speaker, there are people now who do not receive either regular or seasonal benefits and who live in small communities or in cities where other problems have come up.
For instance in my riding the people of two cities are hard-pressed because of the closing of industries which were operating there some time ago. Therefore civic authorities are quite unable to look after the unemployed who do not receive regular or seasonal benefits and who need something to live on. Of course, this matter comes under provincial jurisdiction, I grant you. It may be that provincial authorities were remiss in their duty, but in cases like these, additional provision should be made to help out those people who have families to support.
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention again to put all the blame on the government for the emergency which has been lasting for some time now. It would not be fair either to suggest that the government must bear the full responsibility for the recession which is felt with more or less intensity here as elsewhere. However, we are justified in criticizing the government policy. Unless evidence is forthcoming that constructive measures will be taken to remedy unemployment or to help those who have not the wherewithal to meet the needs of their families, we shall keep pressing the government and insist that steps be taken as soon as possible.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), in the course of this debate made a review of the measures taken by his government since June 10, 1957, and which were meant to promote employment and help the unemployed. At the time of that discussion, he showed great displeasure with the opposition's criticism. He does not appreciate the opposition pointing out the government's weak points.

The Address-Mr. Dumas
Well, Mr. Speaker, we criticize the government in the first place because of the exaggerated promises it made to obtain the popular vote. We also criticize it for having been so slow to take action once it had obtained power; we find fault with the government because most of the measures it did take have proven inadequate. We have protested, we are still protesting and we will go on protesting, against the weakness with which the government has tackled the job in hand, which was to create economic conditions conducive to higher employment throughout Canada.
You will recall that there was reference to great public works. We were given to understand that if the Conservative party came into power, a new public works program would be launched, whereas, in fact, the famous billion dollar program was merely the continuation and completion of projects undertaken by the former government, and we are still waiting for the government to announce that those major works will be undertaken in conjunction with the provinces and private industry. There was also a reference to a large scale plan to settle the far north, although the government must have known that, for the time being at least, such an undertaking was impracticable. That the government should pursue the airmapping work already started in the north, finish the aerial photography work in that area; do topographical, geological and other surveys of the more accessible areas; that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources should set up a development program for the future, well and good. We agree and have no objection whatever. But to claim that to speed up the country's development, we will have to leave unexplored and, of course, undeveloped thousands of square miles located more to the south, and go into an area where transportation is difficult, water power lacking and where for many reasons it will be extremely difficult to attract the necessary labour, that, Mr. Speaker, is quite another matter.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock, when the debate was adjourned, I was saying that the development program in northern 
Canada, as understood by the government, is not practical, at least for the time being; that it is a program which cannot, for instance, promote the nation's economy, and provide more jobs. For that reason, I said that, there again, the population has been somewhat misled. I said also that we would favour the idea of the government undertaking research projects of all kinds and preparing a program for the future, and that we are fully of the opinion that the Canadian north can be developed later, on a large scale.
That is why I say that, for the moment, if we wish to spur the country's economy, provide jobs, promote fuller development of our known natural resources which are located in easily accessible places, the government should turn its attention farther south, to easily accessible districts, such as the southern Yukon and the Northwest Territories, the northern areas of the western provinces, northern Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland, since there is there ample space where the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources could, by itself or in co-operation with the provinces, according as to whether the territories or the provinces are concerned, carry on their work.
This brings me to suggest another government project, that is the construction of access roads to put within easy reach the natural resources located more to the south, a project which naturally should be implemented in co-operation with the provinces.
In my opinion, such a project is in keeping with plain common sense; it is applicable, and if it were carried on with vigour, it could prove a practical way of providing more jobs and of spurring the economy throughout the country.
However, this access roads construction program has remained in abeyance, Mr. Speaker, because of the government's failure to call, as it should have done, a conference of parties interested in such a project.
It is true that there has been correspondence with the provincial authorities concerned. It is also true that last week it was announced in the press that possibly within a month, the province of Ontario will be signing an agreement with the federal government. However, as this method of communicating by letter with the provinces is much too slow and quite ineffective, and since it is important that at least a majority of the provinces agree to such a plan,

the government should have used other methods.
However, there is still time to correct the situation, and as the saying goes, better late than never. The government should first revise its plan so as to make it more flexible and less costly for the provinces. Then a conference of the provincial and federal ministers concerned should be called as soon as possible, and at such a conference the ministers might lay the foundations of such a plan and decide how to go ahead with it.
I should like to mention to the house, as an illustration, a development project which is just being started in our area, more specifically at lake Matagami, in the constituency of my good friend the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Martel).
Hardly more than a year ago, about one hundred miles north of the cities of Amos and Senneterre, a group of syndicated mining firms discovered a rich deposit of base metals, a few miles south of the great Matagami lake. The proven ore content of this deposit has since been established at 25 million tons, with a total value of over $600 million. Needless to say that immediately after this discovery, large numbers of mining firms invaded this area, with the result that there have been three other discoveries, also very substantial, of base metal deposits of still undetermined value.
The area can be reached only by air. Development, therefore is slow, difficult, and above all very costly. Fortunately, last fall, the firms involved reached an agreement with the provincial government, and the government is now building a winter road fifty miles long. There remains a distance of about 23 miles to be built by the mining firms. In a few days, Mr. Speaker, this road will be open to traffic.
This low-cost winter road will make it possible to develop an area where there is a great wealth in base metals. Of course, soon we will have to build a permanent hardsurfaced road and a railway branch line about 50 miles long that will be linked to the C.N.R. line between Senneterre and Lake St. John, via the Chibougamau region.
Incidentally, I want to remind the house that this latter railroad was built under the former government. It must be realized that the lake Matagami ore will provide much freight to this C.N.R. branch line and
The Address-Mr. Dumas that, in the near future, it will become one of the most profitable branch lines in Canada.
Everybody knows that in a few years, and I repeat, in a few years only, in no more than a decade, there will be a well organized population of more than 10,000 people in the Matagami area.
There is fertile land up there and, if the provincial government would take the trouble to do so, in a few years, it could surely settle 200 or 300 or even more farmers who could benefit from the proximity and development of this new industrial centre.
That is not all. This development, perhaps modest at the beginning, is bound to thrive, and I predict that in a few years, there will be many base metals mines in the Matagami area. It is one of the most promising mining areas of the province of Quebec and, perhaps, of the whole of Canada. Curiously enough, the soil of this region is also very rich. Because outcrops are few, prospecting is rather difficult. The overburden varies in thickness from a few feet to more than 300 feet.
So, it is not surprising that many people are inclined to say that this mining area should have been discovered long ago. Well, it is precisely because outcrops are few, and the overburden varies in depth from a few feet up to 300 feet, that these mineral deposits could not be discovered earlier. We had to use modern methods and to make geophysical, magnetic and electromagnetic surveys to locate these deposits and, today, we have to make expensive diamond borings to confirm the findings of these geophysical and electromagnetic surveys and to prove that there are really mineral deposits there.
Because of the richness of the soil in that area, Father Henri Cloutier predicted, as reported in an article entitled The Kingdom of Matagami, published in Relations of March 1947, the expansion that would take place some day in the Matagami lake district:
The Matagami lake basin, with its vast forests, waterways and lakes, is the greatest untapped reservoir of arable land remaining in Quebec; in other words, it is the only significant area available to us for the launching of a great and progressive enterprise. Suppose you are told to settle, in the shortest possible time and at the lowest cost, from 100,000 to 200,000 young people and families, overflow of old parishes-
One could say that they are now unemployed.

The Address

Mr. Dumas
-suppose you are also asked to provide for the prosperity of the 50,000 settlers who are now in Abitibi. The proposal is ambitious but reasonable, and it is imperative.
And then, Father Cloutier goes on to explain that all these people should be directed toward the Matagami lake district. A little farther down, he writes:
Is the present Abitibi an obstacle barring the real route to the north? Or is it a springboard from where we should start occupying the real important district, i.e. the kingdom of Matagami, and set up the capital, which cannot be set up elsewhere, since nature decided so?
Well, Mr. Speaker, this article clearly shows, in a few words, the importance of the Matagami lake district.
Here is an area where it would be possible to settle hundreds of thousands of people. The mere construction of a railroad will make it possible to develop rich ore deposits which, when mines go into operation at some future date, will provide employment for thousands of workers.
Why can't the federal government reach an agreement with the government of the province of Quebec for the construction, in the Matagami area, of a whole network of winter roads to make prospecting easier and less costly, and to speed up research in the entire area? Last year, a few hundred men found employment in the Matagami area. Yet, as I mentioned a moment ago, the only means of transport was by air. Knowing the cost of such transportation, and the difficulty of moving large groups of men by air, we find that now that there is a road, a winter road, more workers will be able to enter the area. Moreover, if a road-building program such as I have mentioned were rapidly carried out, I am sure that before 1960 over a thousand workers could find jobs in the Matagami area.
Why couldn't the federal government also do the same in the accessible parts of the Yukon, in the Northwest Territories, and the northern areas of the western provinces and Ontario, and in other parts of the province of Quebec, as well as in Labrador, in Newfoundland and in the maritimes?
Mr. Speaker, this program makes sense, but the federal government must show more daring. The government must convince the provinces that current unemployment has to be checked, and that this is one way to do it. There are many other ways of checking
[Mr. Dumas.1
unemployment. Perhaps it cannot be stopped completely, but surely there are means of improving the situation.
I recognize that a program such as I have described will not provide employment for hundreds of thousands of workers, but if this were done throughout the country-and there is no reason for not doing it-in the Yukon, for instance, in the Northwest Territories, in the southern part of those territories, in the Peace River district, in northern Manitoba, where the International Nickel Company is operating a nickel mine of unprecedented capacity, at Mohawk and Thompson lakes, -and there are indeed other lands or parts of land that may hold very rich mineral deposits; if all would co-operate and if the federal government would call a conference here, in Ottawa, of provincial ministers of mines and colonization-I mention provincial ministers of colonization because this is very important, particularly in the region like that of Matagami, where, for instance, the land is fertile-if we could have, side by side, the mining industry, the lumbering industry, and agriculture, we could be sure to make good. We would make good because those who would settle as farmers in this area could, in their spare time, find employment in the industry, because they would live close to large centres.
As I said earlier, in a few years we would have in the Matagami area, a community of some 10,000 people. Well, it means something to have such a large community. It is large enough to help 200 to 300 farmers to make a living. So, we should make a careful study of the situation and revise the methods used to this day, particularly in the field of colonization.
You cannot expect today to go up to a man and say: "You are going to settle in range so-and-so of such-and-such township; then, you will build your own log camp and you will clear the first acres". You can't do that. The government has the responsibility, today, of finding places in which to settle new farmers. The government should clear the first acres, build comfortable houses, where these people could live with a certain degree of satisfaction. Then, it would be much easier to sell them those lands at $5,000, $8,000 or $10,000, if necessary, on easy terms, than to give them the lands, in the form of tenancy tickets, at the low price of $10 or $15. Then many people would settle out

there, farm that land and make this particular region grow. This could be done everywhere in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the government should think things over and make arrangements so that we might start first by speeding up the development of easy-to-reach regions, where there are adequate natural resources for many years to come.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I wish first to congratulate the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Second, your fine record as Speaker of this house has pleased everyone. As we all know, you bring honour to this parliament. I also wish to join with other hon. members in congratulating the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea) has been a great help to me since I came to Ottawa, and I wish to thank him very much.
The House of Commons, I have been told, is big league, and it did not take long to establish who are the big leaguers. Your fame, Mr. Speaker, was known to me before I left the coast and now, having seen you work, I know why you have the admiration and respect of all parties. Before coming to Ottawa I thought of the House of Commons as being two rows of trenches separated by a no man's land. 1 admire your courage, Mr. Speaker, sitting as you do between the rows. I was of the opinion that a member never crossed this no man's land except to join another party. You can well imagine my amazement when I noticed members of the opposition going across from time to time and talking to the various ministers. However, that was last session; this session I have not seen it happen. There has certainly been a change somewhere along the line.
This being my first speech in the House of Commons I feel very much as I did when I first went solo in an aircraft, the difference being that now at least I shall not be hurt. The kindness of members of the House of Commons to a member making his first speech is traditional and, as in the case of the aircraft, if I keep my nose out of the dirt I will come to no harm.
1 wish now to pay tribute to two former members of this house who have passed away. I speak first of William Val Yacula.
The Address-Mr. Matthews In the short time I knew him I became aware of his many qualities, and I am confident that had he continued he would have contributed greatly to the welfare of Canada as an elected member of the House of Commons. He was a very friendly man, and I am pleased to say that in the very short time I knew him I was able to call him Val.
It was my good fortune last session to share an office with the late Edward Russell Lock-yer. Ed Lockyer was the type of man who should be elected to parliament. In Toronto he gave as much of his life as he could to the service of that city, being always active in performing such services as were for the advancement and betterment of his fellow Canadians. We can well understand why Ed was elected and, if he so wishes, I know he will be elected to the grand lodge above.
As hon. members know, I represent the constituency of Nanaimo, which is that central part of Vancouver island extending from Englishman river on the north to Cobble Hill on the south, including the beautiful gulf islands. As a candidate it is necessary that you become a salesman or, better still, a super salesman, and your first selling job is to sell yourself to the people of your constituency. Then, after you are elected you come to Ottawa and sell your constituency to your fellow members of parliament. I could do a real selling job among my colleagues in this chamber if it were possible to take them all by jet aircraft to beautiful Nanaimo and the islands. It would take about six hours to make the flight to Nanaimo.
Nanaimo is known as the gateway to Vancouver island, and all roads lead to this gateway. There are 21 ferry sailings daily to and from Nanaimo by the finest ferry ships in the world. In 1957 the ferry boats carried 1,710,934 passenger cars and 201,383 freight cars from Vancouver to Nanaimo, and in the same year 61,000 tourists registered at the chamber of commerce. Seven hundred and twenty-three foreign vessels and 3,471 coastal ships cleared Nanaimo in the same year.
It was very interesting during the recess to have the Minister of Fisheries in Nanaimo and to have the pleasure of spending a day with him looking over the wonderful biological station there. If any hon. member should have a mind to travel and see something of interest I would suggest that he visit this marvellous station. They have a model

The Address-Mr. Matthews there of Hecate strait. This is an exact model. The tides go in and out, and it all happens at the same hours as the tides in Hecate strait itself.
Anglo Canadian Timber Products operate a sizeable industry in Nanaimo and of course, as hon. members all know, MacMillan and Bloedel Ltd. have a tremendously big pulp mill there. Sometimes between 400 and 500 big fishing boats are in the harbour, and that sight in itself is certainly well worth seeing. We have two branches of the legion there, Canadian Legion No. 10 and Canadian Legion No. 256. I just mention these two facts in order to give hon. members some idea of the variety of industries and interests we have represented.
As to sports in Nanaimo, we have a famous team there which won quite a number of hockey championships, and it was two years ago in the Maple Leaf gardens that a Nanaimo team won the Mann cup for Canadian senior lacrosse. This is the first time the Mann cup has ever been won in the east by a western team though, to be honest about it, I must add that we did bring some very fine boys from the province of Ontario who like Nanaimo so well that they are living there, have their families there and intend to stay.
At this point I might mention that sport, to me, is a very important thing. I was pleased to hear recently that the John Labatt company under Mr. J. W. Murray are sponsoring that lacrosse team this year. If any big company in Canada wants to do a real service I would say that the sponsoring of good hockey teams, baseball teams and lacrosse teams is one of the finest forms of advertising and one of the best things they could do as Canadian firms.
We have a very nice ice rink in Nanaimo, and we have a curling rink, too. Anyone interested in curling should remember that we have eight rinks on Vancouver island and, as I said, we have one in Nanaimo. The fishing there is tremendous. I will not dwell on this, but I recommend anyone here to go out and try some of our fishing when the session is over.
I must thank the hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Grills), who invited us to go over to the Hull arena yesterday to see the Belleville Macs play against the Hull senior team. It was very enjoyable, and I might mention that the coach of this Belleville team comes from New Westminster. Going back some years to the period when I had first a juvenile team and then a junior team, I can remember

that he was always a thorn in the side of our club at that time. I should like to wish Ike Hildebrand of the Macs team every luck in the world championship games.
Continuing this tour of my constituency, from Nanaimo I should like to take hon. members out by bus, if it were possible, on a tour of this beautiful country. They would call at the city of Ladysmith. I wish they could go from there into the logging camps and see the actual logging conditions, the tremendous diameters they take out, trees which are the finest and largest in the world. I might remark at this time that in my constituency they brought out a 225-foot Douglas fir spar tree, about five feet at the butt, as I remember. That was sent over to England, and hon. members can imagine that tremendous 16-ton spar tree going over to England. I would be very happy if we had one on the lawn in front of this building. They also have Canadian Legion No. 171 and the Comox Logging and Railway Company.
Leaving Ladysmith we would then go up to Cowichan lake and Honeymoon bay. Here you would find large scale logging operations and sawmills that would amaze you. If you were driving through here in the summer and had a fishing rod in your car you probably could not resist the temptation to do a little fishing, because it is a sportsman's paradise. At Cowichan lake there is Canadian Legion No. 210. At Honeymoon bay is situated the Western Forest Industries Limited and the Cowichan Copper Company. The latter produced ore amounting to $1,200,000 in 1958. There is also the Mayo Lumber Company at Honeymoon bay.
Leaving this area we would then go down to the beautiful city of Duncan, that will delight and interest all hon. members. I am sure you would find you would want to spend at least a day here examining the many historic points of interest. There is an Indian reservation nearby, and the famous Cowichan Indian sweaters come from here. There is a curling rink and a progressive chamber of commerce which does a splendid job. Hillcrest Lumber Company is situated here, and there is Canadian Legion No. 53.
Leaving Duncan we cut back to Crofton and go through the new and up to date pulp mill that was recently opened there by British Columbia Forest Products Limited, and then go on to Chemainus to inspect the large lumber mill and watch the workers cut Douglas fir and load cargo freighters with British Columbia lumber for all parts of the world. MacMillan and Bloedel Limited is also located there, and there is Canadian Legion No. 191.

We now come to a most exciting point in our tour, because we now return to Nanaimo where we board a power boat and take a cruise through the beautiful gulf islands. I am sure hon. members would enjoy the thrill provided by passing through Dodd narrows where the tide runs at from ten to twelve knots. In a small craft this makes the journey an exciting one. The international cruiser race is held practically every year commencing at Seattle and concluding at Nanaimo. There can be as many as 125 cruisers in the race, and many may reach the narrows at approximately the same time. It is very exciting to watch the small boats bobbing in the water like corks, almost brushing one another as they speed ahead. Few can resist the excitement the race provides.
As we continue our tour, Gabriola island will be on our left. This area was first settled by people who came from California and from England years ago. They are a fine and happy people. We then pass on to Galiano island and cross over to Mayne island, where we spend a few hours. Reluctantly we leave these pleasure spots and proceed to Saturna island for another interesting event, the annual lamb barbecue. A few years ago a small group of perhaps 25 people from cruisers that had come up from the United States and British Columbia met and held a lamb barbecue. It is now an annual event and the attendance has increased considerably. Games and various other activities are now associated with the barbecue, and it is a source of pleasure to many tourists. There is excellent fishing, and some fine summer resorts are located on the islands.
From Saturna we proceed to north and south Pender islands before docking at Ganges harbour, which is on the south end of Saltspring island. I had the pleasure of attending the opening of the modern hospital at Ganges harbour, and it is indeed a wonderful building. We then go to Bedwell harbour where commencing this summer a customs and excise office will be situated. Pleasure boats coming up from the United States will be able to dock there before cruising on. There are many fine things to see in this area including hotels, golf courses and ferries. I might add that as many as 800 or 900 pleasure boats pass through Nanaimo every year coming from various parts of the United States. The people of Ganges harbour are active and progressive. They have a branch of the Canadian Legion and a chamber of commerce. They do not hesitate to write me about their problems, and all hon. members appreciate it when their constituents acquaint them with their difficulties rather than allowing them to become the cause of unrest.
The Address-Mr. Matthews
It will be difficult to get you to leave any of these island beauty spots, but we must be on our way back and I know that all hon. gentlemen will want to return to Nanaimo and the island. And now permit me to tell you something about the people who live in this riding.
We have there our pioneers who helped build our country. We have war veterans who fought for our country. We also have young Canadians who are eager to build a better Canada. We also have a large number of industries, including our commercial fishing, our many logging camps and sawmills and at the present time two large pulp mills. We have loggers who can handle the largest timber and log the steepest grades of any loggers in the world. If I wanted practical advice on commercial fishing, logging, lumber milling, road building or power development, I could get it from men who not only know how to do it but who can do it. I have had a flow of letters from the people in my constituency demanding a humane method for the slaughter of animals. I assure them that this matter is of great concern to me and I will do all I can to support their appeal.
I should like to compliment the hon. member for Victoria for his stand with respect to the right of old age pensioners to receive their pension even after leaving Canada, and I will support this position. When a pension of any form is given it should be an earned pension. Canadian pensions given in the form of old age pensions or pensions to members of the civil service, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the armed services are well earned pensions. All these people are shareholders in the building of Canada and are entitled to draw their dividends when they retire.
In the building of Canada a number of machines have come into being from time to time to assist in this work. As a boy I can remember the stone boats used on the farms. These were used to clear rocks from the land so it could be tilled and cultivated. It was a most useful article. There was also a machine called a fertilizer spreader and, of course, there was a seed spreader, probably created by Massey-Harris, and these too were useful inventions. When I walked up to the House of Commons just a week ago I saw a new machine on the street, a truck belonging to the public works department of the city of Ottawa. It had a chain drive from the rear wheel hub which when thrown into gear spread sand on the streets. It had a sign on the back that read "sand spreader". But I was to see another new machine that same day. It was a machine put out by a desperate group of left-overs, a new Liberal machine called a "gloom spreader". This machine,

The Address-Mr. Matthews so far as thinking Canadians are concerned, is about as effective in this day and age as the Wright brothers' first aircraft would be on a trip to the moon.
If we read back in history we find that all dictators in their attempts to conquer have used fear as their weapon. They used fear not only on the armies they were fighting but they carried as much fear and terror as they could to the civilian population. Even women and children were exposed to as much of this fear as could be directed their way. Any political party that attempts to take over and control Canada, using fear as a weapon, will only destroy itself. Fear has always been used as a weapon to kill faith. A party that destroys the faith of its own people also kills the faith of other countries, and that goes a long way toward causing a depression.
At this point I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister for having visited so many countries on his tour. Other countries with which we trade and that wish to trade with us are watching and looking for good reasons to have faith in Canada. It is our duty and purpose to supply them with reasons for having faith in our great country.
It took no great vision, no great courage, for us to make this six-hour trip to Nanaimo; but when we think of the pioneers who came by ship, taking months to make the trip, when we think of the hardy people who came from eastern Canada across the country by wagon train or later by railway, with no hospitals, no unemployment insurance, nothing but their great faith, their courage and their desire to build a new Canada, I wonder how any of us can be uncertain about the future of Canada. In the descendants of those pioneer builders of our nation we still have men and women of faith, courage and ability; we still have a country second to none in national resources. All that the people have been waiting for is a government with vision and faith, and we all agree that on March 31, 1957, the voters of Canada supplied just that.
It should be the purpose of this government to get on with the job. Our pioneers, the builders of Canada, our senior citizens and our war veterans should receive more than just enough to live on. We know that the wage earners of Canada want these old people to have a good standard of living, and I will always work to achieve this end.
No doubt, Mr. Speaker, it is very much of an ordeal for hon. members of the opposition to sit in this parliament, but to them I say "Be of good cheer". When you are old you will look back to these days and will be able proudly to say, "I sat in parliament when
[Mr. Matthews.}
Canada's greatest development took place under the leadership of Prime Minister John Diefenbaker and the Progressive Conservative banner."
