speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of the amendment as amended; and to refresh the memories of hon. members, because of the diversity of topics discussed to date. I am going to read the amendment as amended by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue):
We respectfully affirm that Your Excellency's advisers, by reason of contradictory and confused policies caused by the absence of social and economic planning, and their failure to provide agriculture with a fair share of the national income, and their further failure to take effective steps to combat inflation, no longer merit the confidence of this house.
Before proceeding, Mr. Speaker, I must say how much it delights me to have my old friend the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, (Mr. Rowe), our topnotch free-enterpriser, sit in his seat this afternoon to listen to the philosophy of the C.C.F.
I want to say that my remarks this afternoon will in particular be related to the absence of provision for economic and social planning in the throne speech, social and economic planning which we in this group think is essential to meet the needs of the unemployed in Canada, the needs of the farmers for markets and the instability that is in our economy at the present time.
We in this group give this government full credit for proposing certain measures that will be of value to Canadians and in some cases, as in the case of farmers, veterans and civil servants, of value to particular groups. However, I must emphasize this. We feel that the political medicine provided in the throne speech lacks the potency required to cure the ancient maladies of inflation, the growing unemployment and the lack of markets that particularly concern all Canadians at this time.
I want to say this, Mr. Speaker. We in this group do not profess to have all the wisdom and all the knowledge but we do think we have a sounder approach to our problems than that proposed by the other parties. We have sat and listened to the speeches of hon. members, and regardless of our differences in economic theory policies we recognize that members of this house, whatever their point of view, are making their contribution from their own particular point of view or lack of understanding and so on.
Speakers on the government benches or the opposition benches have used what I would term a welter of words to criticize one another, and it has been quite a skirmish

at times. The debate seems to oscillate these days between a lullaby and a baseball game. In our opinion the criticism of one another's policies on the whole has been somewhat superficial, and that is because there is no fundamental difference in approach to social and economic problems between the old parties. I think that is a correct statement. They are both parties supporting a so-called free enterprise system which no longer exists. However, I must say that a few speakers have recognized and mentioned the disease of unemployment, but they have failed to offer a remedy or, shall I say, a fundamental remedy. They have in each case-and I listened with interest on two or three occasions-presented their problem to the government only. They stopped short then with respect to offering or making some definitive and concrete proposals.
Both old-line parties proposed various degrees of tinkering with and patching up the present incorrectly termed free-enterprise system, which is more and more being revealed as the days go by-and I am sure the future will emphasize it-as nothing more or less than economic anarchy.
What is the situation we face today in this house? I am sure that hon. members here, when they speak on this question, are conscious of the unemployed and of the difficulties of the farmers, of the small businessmen and of other groups in our society. What is the situation we face in Canada some 14 years after the second world war, after one of the greatest and most prosperous periods in our history? We all know that there are approximately half a million unemployed in our country at this time, and a large surplus of unsold stocks of agricultural products and industrial commodities. While that condition exists in Canada at this time we all know that about half the people of the world go to bed hungry every night, and that great numbers are in need of the commodities which we have in such great supply. I think that is a fair statement of the situation.
I rise this afternoon particularly to emphasize the fact that the C.C.F. offers a constructive alternative to meet the present economic dilemma. We have mentioned our policies on many occasions in past years. We think that particularly on the throne speech we should re-emphasize our approach to the situation in view of the remarks we have made all throughout the years and their particular application to the present circumstances.
Our alternative to the policies offered by the government and the official opposition parties is known generally as democratic
The Address-Mr. Herridge socialism. I can see the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe beginning to blink already. In other words, that means a consciously planned economy with the consent and cooperation of the people of this country. We in this group believe we can have a planned economy and have all the basic freedoms we enjoy at this time.
I will come back later to policy, Mr. Speaker, to indicate the lack of confidence that is growing among business and industrial leaders in Canada, in the United States and in other countries at the present time over the effects of Soviet competition and competition from other countries. I am going to quote very briefly from the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, January 24. I think this is rather remarkable coming from people who resent government interference with free enterprise. They firmly believe in free enterprise. Very often they have criticized the aged, the ill and the disabled for requesting higher pensions in order to have a decent standard of living or some opportunity to enjoy national health insurance and things of that sort. They say, "Oh, oh, there they are again running to the government."
What are these people doing at this time? They are in a dilemma. These free enterprisers are running to the governments of their respective countries, as they have done in Canada before, to bail them out. The article is headed, "United States Business Worried by Soviet Competition", and reads as follows:
American business leaders are said to be giving serious consideration to the prospect that rapidly growing communist competition-
Fancy them being frightened of competition. Why, that is the basis of their whole lives but they are frightened of it now.
-in world trade markets might result in the fairly near future in the government moving into a field hitherto regarded as sacred to private enterprise. The research institute of America, a private organization which claims contacts in the communist world as well as in high level United States circles, has circulated among United States business leaders a "report to management"-
Always to management, not to the people.
-which claims Washington already is considering some sort of government take-over in the foreign trade field.
Then there is the heading, "Figures Cause Dismay."
The report, which contains statistics from Russia and communist China indicating that the two big communist powers are rapidly overtaking the United States in almost every production field, says the surge in the east has caused "particular dismay" in Washington with the result that "senior United States officials have been seriously considering how to make politically acceptable"-

The Address-Mr. Herridge That means acceptable to the business strata of the community.
-"the establishment of a government foreign trade monopoly"-
My goodness, Mr. Speaker, we have advocated that in this house for a number of years and it was anathema to the Conservative and Liberal parties. It was an invasion of free enterprise. However, these gentlemen, who are now in a dismayed state of mind, are going to suggest a government foreign trade monopoly.
-"which might be able to compete"

"Might".
-"with the communist monopolies on something approaching equal terms. It is not too much to say that continuance of communist economic growth and the increase of 'unfair' communist price competition"-
Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, how certain business elements in this country opposed the resale price maintenance act as it interfered with what they termed fair competition?
-"could cause the end of private enterprise in international trade in the years immediately ahead."
What a disaster!
Soviet goals in the current seven-year plan would surpass the United States in most economic fields by 1965, the report says. Even if Russia fell far short of these goals it "would nonetheless develop into a much more formidable competitor in world markets than it is now."
The economic advances would be over and above the production and development of weapons in the military field in which, the report concedes, "the Russians are clearly ahead of the United States."
So they admit they are ahead of them in a military sense and overtaking them rapidly in an economic sense. Then follows the headings, "Red China Menace."
Red China's transformation, however, is regarded as even more portentous than that of Russia. "Peiping's staggering goal", the United States leaders are told, "is nothing less than the transformation of China's primitive economy into a modern industrial heavyweight capable of competing with either or both the Soviet union and the United States within ten years."
The entire report, with one exception, is one of pessimism for the future of business in the western world. The exception is the "underlying possibility" that Russia might be forced into seeking an alliance with the west because of fear of "the surging Far Eastern threat of military and economic dominance."
As usual they are hoping that some quarrel between some people or nations will provide the answer to their difficulties. I am serious about this, Mr. Speaker. We continually talk of free enterprise in Canada. In that connection I want to quote a sentence or two from an editorial that appeared in the Globe and Mail of Thursday, January 22. We must not forget that generally speaking the Globe and Mail supports the policies of the government of the day, and it is a paper I read with 
a great deal of interest. This is what I find in one editorial in the Globe and Mail in our free enterprise Canada:
This newspaper's quest for facts was occasioned by increasing evidence that Canada was being negotiated into economic as well as military servitude to the United States.
I think there is a great deal of validity to that statement. What further evidence do we want than the refusal of Alcan to sell aluminum to China after receiving an export permit from the government? Does that company accept no responsibility to Canada as a whole? Does it accept no responsibility to its employees? It refuses this opportunity to trade. For what reason? Because it is contrary to the policies of the United States state department. We are being influenced from that direction. They do that while hundreds of their own employees are unemployed and seeking work.
As I proceed with my argument let me emphasize once again the fact that we in the C.C.F. are strongly opposed to the political dictatorship of communism and the economic dictatorship of monopoly capitalism, the type of dictatorship in North America which is providing increasing evidence that Canada is being negotiated into economic as well as military servitude to the United States.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, the C.C.F. offers a democratic alternative policy based on a study and knowledge of Canadian history, Canadian psychology and the present circumstances. We propose a dual or mixed economy based on constitutional and parliamentary procedures. We believe that there are these two great forces in the world and that a clash will inevitably result in the days to come between what I might term the extreme right and the extreme left in politics and economics unless we take some middle course and utilize our intelligence, our constitution and our parliamentary procedures to find another program that will give us the results we seek.
First of all I might mention that we in the C.C.F. recognize that the satisfactory development of a dual or mixed planned economy in Canada rests essentially on co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. That is essential. Otherwise we will not have the success that is necessary. It is up to the leaders of the federal and provincial governments to forgo their petty political differences and their wish at times to gain political advantage for the welfare of the Canadian people as a whole in the development of such a policy as we propose.
When I refer to a mixed or dual economy I mean exactly that. We believe that we have got to have the conscious planning that will provide an opportunity for the development

of public enterprise in the federal, provincial and municipal fields according to the circumstances of the time and to the advantage of the Canadian people as a whole. We believe in a great expansion of co-operative ownership and the development of the co-operative philosophy. There is nothing like the experience of working in a co-operative movement, whether it is a producers' co-operative, a consumers' co-operative or a credit union, to give one a good understanding of the administrative principles of democracy. I think it is good groundwork for anyone seeking to serve in the political field.
We in this group also believe that there is a tremendous opportunity for what we would term legitimate private enterprise. We mean private enterprise where a genuine element of competition comes into play, where the consumer is protected by a measure of genuine competition and where the enterprise, whether industrial, engaged in distribution or in service, is rendering a necessary service to the community.
Sometimes I am criticized by some of my socialist friends for taking the stand to which I am about to refer. I do not mean the group behind me. I am thinking of persons whose views are more doctrinaire in some respects. There is a distinction to be made between the effect of foreign investment in a country and internal investment. Foreign investment means that at the end of the year there is an export of capital from Canada and a net loss of total wealth to the Canadian people. Canadian investment, local or community investment, means that an industry through operations carried on, perhaps not directly in line with our philosophy and theories, results in no net loss to Canada in wealth because the profits are re-invested in our country. There is, therefore, no drain on, shall I say, our total wealth by Canadian ownership.
Now, I want to emphasize this. While we have been criticized for emphasizing the need for planning, I must say that planning is something which is essential in a modern society. What we are concerned about is that we do not have the planning as a result of the corporate state, but that we have planning by the people and for the people. It is for that reason we are concerned about developments in our country. I should like to quote from a letter which I read in the Globe and Mail. I see the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) is rather amused at my reading the Globe and Mail so frequently, but there is a very thoughtful approach to the present situation in this letter. I quote in part from this letter to the Globe and Mail of Saturday, January 24:
The Address-Mr. Herridge
The real reason for the development of the new system of state-aided enterprise, which we are now enjoying, is the basic fact that production has overwhelmed the old order where supply and demand could indeed exert its influence.
That is one reason why we are not overcoming inflation. There are certain rigidities in our economy today as a result of price control and as a result of wages that do not permit the law of supply and demand to work as usual. It is not possible for anybody today to correct the price situation by lowering the workers' wages.
What we now witness is a frantic effort on the part of government to maintain private enterprise and at the same time nullify the effects of competition, which was the heart of the private enterprise system.
Obviously it is absurd to speak of free enterprise in this context, but it doesn't appear to have deterred anyone. None of our major political parties have faced up to this truth, nor has there been any concern with the inevitability of changes in our political and economic pattern as a result of this dichotomy.
Free enterprise has gone not because of the actions of wicked radicals, but because the inherent imbalance of capitalist production and the growing technology that accompanied it have forced upon the state a set of what first appeared to the politicians as a series of ad hoc measures designed to relieve immediate crises, but which now show themselves to be permanent in their nature. Production outpaces consumption at such a rate and brings with it such dangerous social implications that the state is forced to step in and take up the surplus. But. of course, this sort of "solution" can only be temporary.
It is therefore not hard to envision that, because of the deficits incurred by the new system of state-aided enterprise, and the psychological effects of the stored surpluses that nobody knows how to get rid of, plus the growing unemployment, the state will move into its next stage-control of prices and production in a manner that will ensure a high rate of profit to the larger units of production, and the control of labour to ensure such profit. That is to say, free enterprise having already ended, and our existing system of state-aided enterprise being only a temporary botch of things, it is inevitable that the corporate state must move into the saddle in an attempt to restore order. In the U.S. first, of course, but we will follow in the usual way.
Some of us may not be enthused over this prospect, but that is the logic of events.
He is quite right; that is the logic of events, in our opinion, unless we are willing to accept very soon some planning based, on democratic procedures. As I said before, co-operation between federal, provincial and municipal governments is essential for success in developing a planned economy.
I am just going to outline what I consider to be one or two of the essential steps. I have not the time to deal with this subject very fully. I do feel that, first of all, we must make sure of our raw materials. We say one of the first steps is a national policy for the conservation and development of natural resources, as a result of co-operation between all levels of government. There is

The Address-Mr. Herridge no use having fiscal policies or other good legislation without having your natural resources conserved and developed, having in mind the need for a constant flow of wealth to meet the needs of the increasing population, and future generations.
What is the present situation? So far as the development of resources in Canada is concerned, it is chaotic, it is wasteful and it is irresponsible. I shall demonstrate why. I would cite the proposals of the government of British Columbia for the development of the Rocky mountain trench, which comprises about one-tenth of the area of British Columbia, by international financiers whose interest is purely profit. They have no interest in the people of British Columbia. Mr. Wenner-Gren came, said how do you do, goodbye, and went away. What would happen with that development? From our point of view, it is an improper development, a wasteful development, that could damage the possibilities for public hydro development on the Columbia. This hydro development would supply the power required in British Columbia for some years to come. It could affect adversely the established mining and lumbering industries in British Columbia.
At the present time we have lead, zinc and other mines closed down for lack of markets. There are sawmills closed down for lack of markets, as well as sawmills operating under great difficulties because of low prices and competition. However, the plans are for this group of financiers to move into British Columbia to develop the Rocky mountain trench, without any concern about the damage it might do to British Columbia's economy. This development would be under monopoly control and would damage the possibility of a sound development of the Columbia river with its hydro resources, and this would constitute a threat to the incomes, to the employment and to the lives of thousands of employees who are working in other industries in the other developed parts of British Columbia. We say that is completely chaotic and irresponsible, development of resources.
Let us look at the expansion in other fields. There is a declining world market in nickel and other metals, and this has been obvious for the last two or three years. While that state of affairs exists, we have the unnecessary expansion and development of nickel, lead and zinc mines, as well as some other metals, without any sense of social responsibility for the welfare of Canadians as a whole or the industries concerned. Some of these activities are entirely unrelated to the welfare of Canadians, having in mind only one thing,

the profits possible from mining or, in some cases, a rise in the value of the stocks.
What other illustrations do we find? What about the closing of the coal mines in Canada without any consultation with the federal or provincial governments? Why did they close the coal mines in Fernie last year? They are owned by a United States corporation. This corporation did not close the coal mines because they were losing money in their total operations. They had mines at Fernie and other points. The corporation closed these mines because they wanted to maintain the rate of profit. Was there any concern for the Canadian communities, the Canadian businessmen or the employees? There was none. Without any consultation with this government or the government of British Columbia, they exercised their judgment in their own interests.
What about the coal mines in Nova Scotia? I listened, I think it was Friday, to the two speeches made by two members from Nova Scotia concerning the closing of the coal mines at Springhill by Dosco, which I understand is now owned by Avro. I was very sympathetic to what they had to say. Before proceeding, I want to say that we in this group heartily support them in their efforts to get something done for these courageous miners who have suffered so much, and whose reward for that suffering is unemployment.
I now want to quote the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) as reported in Hansard because it is obvious that these members have witnessed the effects of an unplanned economy and of the irresponsibilities of large corporations at this time. As reported at page 278 of Hansard, this is what the hon. member for Cumberland has to say in part:
Here is a company with 40 subsidiaries. Yet they cannot find anything, so they say, that they can place in this town that has these courageous men. What kind of company is this that would have this feeling and yet go into our area and tell us that they are going to make our future better? If this is the way in which they make our future better, I do not want any part of it.
We congratulate the hon. member for sticking up for the people he represents. We realize that he is a member of the Progressive Conservative party giving expression to the fact that he recognizes that this large corporation does not think of the employees and the people of Springhill first but that it thinks of the total rate of profit first.
I should also like to quote from the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir) as reported at page 286 of Hansard of Friday, January 23 as follows:
This gigantic corporation has the future destiny of Nova Scotians in the palm of its hand.

Not the government of Nova Scotia, Mr. Speaker, but this gigantic corporation.
It is gigantic. It appears that the more gigantic a corporation becomes, the more ruthless it can be.
We have said that on this side of the house for a good number of years, and a great deal of displeasure was expressed on the other side of the house on occasion. Members thought we were exaggerating. This is a Progressive Conservative member giving expression to his opinion of the delinquencies of large corporations. He says this:
It appears that the more gigantic a corporation becomes, the more ruthless it can be. I am sure that all members in this house and all Canadians who contribute through taxation to the development of industry are awaiting the answers to these and many other questions.
I may say that so are a good many people in Canada. May I give just one concluding illustration of the chaotic way in which other services are carried on without any sense of responsibility to the nation as a whole by capitalist interests. This has not to do with the development of natural resources but with our railway transportation. What about the action of the C.P.R. with respect to the reduction of its passenger service on the Kettle Valley railway to one Budd car twice a week? Here is the C.P.R., the parent company of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company which has made hundreds of millions of dollars in profits which have benefited the C.P.R. This Kettle Valley line of the company, because of the large tonnage it hauls from Consolidated Mining and Smelting company's mines and plants, is an extremely profitable line. Regardless of the needs and wishes of 100,000 people who live in southeastern British Columbia and who produce the wealth of that country which provides the business for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the company reduced the passenger railway service to twice a week with one Budd car.
What are the people asking for? All they are asking for is that there be attached to this Budd car a sleeping car for the older people and mothers with children and a cafe car so that they can get something satisfactory to eat while on the way to Vancouver or to the interior. That is all they are asking. What has happened? The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) went to see Mr. Crump, the president of the Canadian Pacific railway. Mr. Crump said no. Who is in control of this country, Mr. Speaker, so far as transportation is concerned? Is it the government of Canada or is it Mr. Crump? We do not believe in that sort of thing. I can say this, Mr. Speaker: when a C.C.F. government gets into office, that sort of situation will be remedied quickly.

An hon. member says "dictatorship". That is his conception. Dictatorship, from his point of view, is the will of the people expressed through parliament rather than through the president of the C.P.R.
In connection with this necessity for a national policy for the development of natural resources, may I say this. I know the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has indicated some interest in this question throughout the years and more particularly recently, as well as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) . I have heard rumours of the possibility of a national conference on conservation being called some time in the future. However, I make this suggestion. I hope that conference will be arranged as soon as possible because I think it is basic. Mistakes can be made in the monetary system and mistakes can be made in the building of structures but when serious mistakes are made in the management of our natural resources they cannot be easily remedied or if they are remedied it can only be done over a long period of time, at a great expense. In the meantime I suggest that surveys, including land use maps, are essential and I suggest that they should be undertaken immediately.
We have the forest inventory in Canada fairly well completed. I understand that we have a fairly accurate survey of our hydro resources. We now need a survey of our land resources and land use maps. This government and the preceding government or the people of Canada, shall I say, have provided land use maps for the people of Pakistan and the people of Ceylon, I believe, under the Colombo plan, and rightly so. If we can do that for these distant countries, surely we can get to work now on these surveys which are so necessary, to the end that when the conference is called it will have the basic information needed to formulate policy. I urge that these land use surveys be carried out at the first opportunity.
Before going on to another aspect of our program, I wish to say this. We hear about the untimely development of natural resources which we criticize, or development purely at the whim of large corporations or the waste in development because of the desire to get into operation as quickly as possible. What do we consider to be a planned expansion of our natural resources? We in this group say that the planned expansion of the economy and its natural resources in a stable manner should be sufficient to absorb the increasing labour force which results from the birth

The Address-Mr. Herridge rate and from immigration as a result of a planned policy in that respect. We would much prefer to see a steady, and stable development of our resources rather than the boom and bust which exists in capitalist society and which in many cases leaves the people who have produced the wealth to suffer afterward.
We also believe that we need a planned fiscal system and planned credit policies to meet the requirements of planned production and development of resources. I am not going into that matter at length this afternoon, but I am just going to say this. The people all across Canada are concerned with inflation, which is another word for the increase in the cost of living. Particularly is this so of the lower income people, those on pensions and incomes of that type and also business people. Nothing can erode the stability of a country faster than continuing inflation. That lack of stability prevents enterprise, saving, investment in houses and all things of that type. I am just going to deal briefly with what are the causes of inflation. One of our members later in this debate will give to the house our policy with respect to meeting the present inflationary situation.
First of all may I say that the inflation after the war without a doubt was caused by accumulated savings during the war coming into the market shortly after the war was completed. I suppose the next serious inflationary period was at the time of the Korean war which provided a scramble for materials, commodities and services. Another factor causing inflation which we must not forget is the large expenditures on defence, a nonproductive activity. Billions and billions of dollars have been poured into defence expenditures which are non-productive or non-wealth-producing. The people who are receiving incomes from defences production are also making claims on the production of the productive workers, and that has had an inflationary effect on the economy since the second world war.
Then, further, we have the wasteful and unplanned development of resources, a scramble for material for industrial requirements and services in our unplanned development, with companies competing against each other for their requirements and services. Another factor has been the increase in speculation in land values because these values have been increasing as a result of the actions of governments, whether federal or provincial, and because of developments which have been taking place in society. Certain people were able to foresee these things, or to have information about them, and to speculate in land values. That is another reason for inflation.


Finally-and I am only able to mention a few of these causes, the large increase in government expenditure has naturally had a bearing on the inflationary trend. It is a very complicated situation, particularly in an unplanned economy, and it cannot be solved without some correlation of our economic activities and planning.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that my time has almost expired, and I am only about half way through. However, we say that a national investment board is desirable in order to direct funds into socially valuable projects. I wish to say in this respect-and I am not suggesting we support the form of the government in question-that we may have something to learn from events in Yugoslavia since the end of the second world war. Yugoslavia is a country which has a population of about the same size as Canada. The postwar government inherited a war-devastated land whose forests and mineral wealth were owned by international financiers. With all their difficulties-and I might explain that the Yugoslav economy is somewhat more flexible than the Soviet-that government was able to produce an economy in which there is not one iota of inflation, and in which there has been no inflation for years, and under which not one Yugoslav citizen who is able to work need be unemployed. Again, I am not suggesting we should accept the Yugoslav political philosophy, but it is evident that this government has made great strides in planning.
I suggest we have something to learn from these people in this respect. Let us get some of their experience tacked on to our natural wealth and to our intelligence and our free institutions. With co-operation we can build in this country the planned economy which is required to give our people the living conditions and stability they seek at this time.

receive a mature presentation in this house. The Canadianism which ran through the speech of the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet will, I think, give rise to a corresponding faith and inspiration in all parts of Canada.
Speaking of the amendment put forward by the C.C.F. group, I have noticed that one of the characteristics was the friendliness displayed between the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the house leader of the C.C.F. group. This friendliness has intrigued me. When I think of the support given to the Leader of the Opposition by the house leader of the C.C.F. group some days ago my mind went back to some of the speeches made by that hon. gentleman when he was back in the west, and I would advise the Leader of the Opposition that he should beware: the things that are said by the C.C.F. leader in the house are not always the same as the things he says when he is out in the country. I have a clipping here dated Thursday, November 27, from the Regina Leader-Post. I will not read it all, but this is a taste of the type of thing we have to bear. This is a report of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) speaking in Regina, and this is what the paper said:
In his criticism of the Liberal party he attacked Liberal leader Lester Pearson saying "Mike Pearson isn't taking the Liberal party anywhere, because Mike Pearson himself doesn't know where he is going."
I have sympathy with the leader of the C.C.F. group here because I know it is not a very pleasant thing to have a crown prince lurking in the background, particularly when the heir apparent is advising labour unions to go out and get all they can, regardless of the consequences to the rank and file of those labour unions, and regardless of the consequences to the Canadian consumer or to Canadians in general. I am sure the hon. member for Assiniboia realizes the predicament he is in. I think he knows that a King Richard on a crusade can be very unhappy with a King John conspiring in the background.
The political peregrinations of the C.C.F. house leader before the session opened carried him to many places and saw him make many strange remarks. One of those places was Springfield, and I know the house will be interested in some of the comments made on that occasion in connection with the byelection. I have here the Winnipeg Free Press of December 11, 1958, from which I intend to read certain extracts to the house so that we may understand precisely what goes on in the west between sessions and be able to compare it with what happens here. This is the quotation:

Federal reinforcements re-entered the Springfield byelection battle on the C.C.F. front here Wednesday in the person of Hazen Argue, and the party's house leader promptly opened a vicious attack on the Tories for not keeping election promises-

But there s no Diefenbaker hula hoop campaigns" this time, said Mr. Schulz. They can't get to the people this time, it's too cold. And when people are left alone they will do the right thing.
"The right thing," he aded, "is to vote for me." If you elect a Conservative you will be endorsing the government's policy.
Mr. Speaker, it was cold in Springfield. Several blizzards during the period of the campaign forced the cancellation of many meetings including those of the premier of Saskatchewan. On election day, when daylight came, the temperature was 24 degrees below zero, according to my information. On election evening when the ballots were counted the C.C.F. ran third. The C.C.F. candidate who had won the seat in 1957 ran third in 1958. The people of Springfield did speak and Canada heard them.

Springfield is a representative riding having a large farm population combined with a large urban population. In the constituency there are trappers, farmers, miners and people in many other occupations. The Liberals threw in their first team and the C.C.F. had at least one member of parliament there during the period of the campaign, or rather a former member of parliament from Saskatchewan. I would like to put on the record for the first time some of the figures which show the thinking in my own province of Saskatchewan. I can do this with some feeling. In 1953, the P.C. vote was 43,677; the Liberal vote was 133,495; the C.C.F. vote was 156,306; others were 20,605; and a total of 317,000 people turned out to vote. Many thought there was no chance of defeating the Liberal government. Some stayed at home; others voted C.C.F. and for other splinter parties. But, in 1957 a change is noted: 90,359 voted P.C.; 118,282 voted Liberal. That was a drop of about 15,000. The C.C.F. dropped to 140,293 and others received 41,292; but this time more turned out, 390,000.
The next spring, 1958, 205,452, 52 per cent, voted P.C.; the Liberals dropped further to 78,124, 19 per cent; the C.C.F. continued their avalanche downward to 112,800; and others were decimated, 2,349, or one per cent. In that winter election 398,000 people in Saskatchewan turned out. Surely, this is some evidence of a tremendous demonstration that something had been wrong and that the people had faith in the Conservative party led by John Diefenbaker, that he would help us do something about it.
For years we had sought for a comprehensive farm program in the west because we knew this was necessary to get at the basic troubles of agriculture. On Friday the house heard the Minister of Agriculture describe the progress to date in that program. I think there is reason, Mr. Speaker, why we held Springfield and why our vote is still going up in western Canada.
I was very pleased myself to hear the Minister of Agriculture tell the house how this year the cost to the farmers rose one per cent but that the gross income rose 10 per cent. This trend of rising costs and declining revenues has been checked; at least we are ahead a little bit. I do know, looking at the figures of Saskatchewan and the prairie provinces generally, that the impact of this government's policies has been most pronounced in the prairies. I could recite to this house not only the impact of the housing program, the impact of the start of the work on the dam, the impact of the northern roads, the impact of the new discoveries in oil and gas, the impact of the potash industry, the impact of all the cattle we are producing, which are up nearly 170,000 head in the last

two years, but the effect of the stabilization prices is giving peace of mind to the farmers of the west for the first time. But all this reciting would not destroy the fact that we know and western Canadians know that the task is not yet completed. Therefore, to assume that we are satisfied with this gain of 10 per cent in the gross revenue or nine per cent in the net is not to prematurely measure this government.
We are pledged to a policy of bringing to the people engaged in agriculture all across the country, not only in the west, a fair share of the national income. To that policy we will remain dedicated and we will keep working with the idea that year by year this thing will pick up and we will be able to give these people, who have borne such a heavy load in this country's growth, their reasonable, fair share in the years to come.

My department has worked out a five year program of accelerating forest research, both basic and applied. The first stages of this go into operation in 1959-60. Following the time-honoured
custom, Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think they did credit to themselves and to their constituencies. I am sure all members of this house are pleased that you, Mr. Speaker, are still with us. We were all disturbed over the rumour that your splendid services might be lost to this house as a result of appointment in another field of the public service of Canada. This other field of the public service has suffered a loss by you remaining here, but we have gained.
The speech from the throne covers many measures to come before this house. However, until those items are presented in legislative form little, if any, detailed information is available to the members of the opposition. The first words in the throne speech advised us of the forthcoming visit of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip. This announcement was welcomed with the greatest of pleasure by all Canadians. The itinerary for the Queen's visit has now been released. While it is realized that all sections of Canada cannot be visited by Her Majesty, it seems only reasonable to expect that in so far as possible the itinerary will include places which the Queen did not visit on her last tour. The itinerary for New Brunswick follows the same course as was followed during the last visit.
Once again, it is found that Her Majesty will not visit the north or northeast part of the province. The citizens of Northumber-land-Miramichi had high hopes they would be given the honour and privilege of welcoming the Queen and her consort. It was hoped the tour would include a motor trip from Fredericton down through the beautiful Miramichi valley to the towns of Newcastle and Chatham, or, as an alternative, a flight by air to the Chatham R.C.A.F. station with the opportunity of a stop-over at government house in South Nelson, the residence of the Hon. J. L. O'Brien, New Brunswick's lieutenant governor, the Queen's representative in our province.
Your efforts, Mr. Speaker, toward putting an end to the reading of speeches are commendable. In the past efforts have failed to bring about the desired result. It is understood and agreed by all parties that this restriction will come into effect following the throne speech debate. This may prove to be a handicap to many members for a time, but in the end it will result in better debates,
330	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. McWilliam even if the choice of words and phraseology suffers somewhat. These efforts toward eliminating the reading of speeches will be watched with keen interest. The results, if achieved, will take time. The use of notes will have to be clearly defined, as the use of copious notes borders closely on the reading of a speech. I am sure all members are anxious to co-operate. However, some latitude will have to be given at the outset, with restrictions being progressively more strictly applied as the session moves forward. If this is not done, many members will be timid about taking part in debate. No doubt this restriction will shorten the length of the debates, but it will not take away any worthwhile contributions.
Two serious problems face Canada today, unemployment and inflation. Despite the statement that unemployment has passed the peak, indications point to serious unemployment during 1959. This is particularly true of the Atlantic provinces. Inflation is also a most serious problem. Despite the statement of a member of the government that inflation and unemployment will have no serious effect on our economy in 1959, I am sure the majority of Canadians do not share that feeling.
Unemployment has been the topic of many Conservative members speaking in this debate as well as of opposition members. Members of all parties from all sections of Canada have called upon the government to take action to combat rising unemployment. Responsible civic organizations and other levels of government across Canada have also called upon the government to take action to combat unemployment. Government action to date has failed to bring about any worthwhile results. For government spokesmen to say that unemployment is on the decline is a misrepresentation of the actual situation. Figures can be twisted around to make the situation look better or worse than it actually is. I doubt that any one would conscientiously say that unemployment is not a serious problem and that the future looks bright. The fast-depleting unemployment insurance fund is proof of the seriousness of the situation, and this depletion of the fund does not show the full impact of unemployment.
The state of unemployment is particularly true in the Atlantic provinces where unemployment figures are rising rapidly to new all-time high records. The official forecasts for March for the maritimes present a bleak picture, based on the continuing loss of markets in mining, forest products and fishing.
Grave concern is felt in the maritime provinces over the plan to keep the St. Lawrence river open on a year-round basis for the


export and import of commodities by water to and from Canada particularly during the winter months. If this plan is put into operation the maritime ports will suffer and serious adverse effects will follow for the economy of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in particular and the maritimes in general. I join with other individuals and groups in protesting against action that will adversely affect our maritime winter ports. If Canada is to survive as a nation of distributed wealth, a plan of "live and let live" must be followed.
Mr. Speaker, we are still waiting for a report on the study of the feasibility of a causeway between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. This survey was started by the Liberal government in 1956 and the people of these provinces are looking for an interim report in view of the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on February 5, 1958-almost a year ago-when he said that the federal government had ordered an immediate engineering study of this project. We wait patiently for an interim report on this matter.
As to the Chignecto canal, the survey was promised and possibly it was started but apparently it bogged down because the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), when asked for a report on this project in this house on Friday last, refused to give one. I am not going to spell out the many advantages that could have been derived from the construction of the Chignecto canal-they have been placed on the record many times in the past- over the years since it was a firm commitment at the time of confederation.
Most of the maritime members of both parties are on record in favour of the early survey and construction of this Chignecto canal. Maritime municipalities, city and town councils, have made representations, for the construction of the Chignecto canal and have urged that the pledge of confederation be honoured as a vital asset to the economy of the maritimes. The need of the Chignecto canal has been recognized in the maritimes over the years. The need is much greater now with the construction of a large oil refinery now under way at Saint John. Proof of the much talked about "aid to the maritimes program" could become a reality by the undertaking of this project.
Since the bill of rights was introduced at the last session, many qualified groups across Canada have expressed the opinion that, desirable as a bill of rights might be, there is no particular rush for the passing of this bill at this session. These groups contend that further study should be given by both houses of parliament at this session, when an exacting

study which the legislation deserves can be given with a view to improving the proposed legislation and at which time representations can be heard from interested groups before a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons.
I turn now to a matter that has caused a good deal of concern and, may I say, a good deal of criticism in the constituency I represent and in all of northeast New Brunswick. At the present time in the constituency which I represent television reception ranges from black-out to snow flurries to rolling pictures to fair reception under ideal conditions. This television service is received from privately owned stations located at Moncton and Saint John. The reason for the poor reception is the fact that these stations are upwards of 100 miles distant. The northeast counties of the province, namely Gloucester and Restigouche, are without television services owing to being an even greater distance away from the stations.
The people of the area which I represent have no quarrel with the privately owned stations with regard to the television reception. On the contrary, they appreciate the programs they are able to receive when conditions are good. They realize that the giving of service to that part of the country, owing to its location and other features, is the responsibility of the C.B.C. The people of Northumberland-Miramichi and the people of northeast New Brunswick feel that they are entitled to their share of the C.B.C. publicly-owned television services. Most Canadians enjoy good C.B.C. television or are located within areas adequately covered by privately-owned stations. Many Canadians have a choice of four or more channels.
Previous requests to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan)-the spokesman for the C.B.C. in parliament-and to the C.B.C. board of governors for C.B.C. television services for northeast New Brunswick have failed to bring about the desired result. The northeast part of New Brunswick can readily be served by the C.B.C. from its system on the west side of the province. There is no good reason why a C.B.C. satellite or repeater or translator, whatever it may be called, cannot be erected on the high ground at the county boundary line between Northumberland and Gloucester counties and be hooked up with the C.B.C. system on the west side of the province. This hook-up would provide good reception in northeast and eastern New Brunswick, an area with a heavy density of population which is now quite without television reception except in the fringe areas where reception is not constant.

I wish now to say a few words with regard to the fishing industry and in particular in connection with fishing on the east coast of Canada. Fishing, as I am sure every hon. member knows, is very important to large sections of the Atlantic provinces, and in this regard problems are mounting almost daily. The most serious aspect of these problems in the Atlantic fisheries is the future of our markets. Newfoundland has a most serious problem in this regard. The Department of Fisheries is striving to improve the lot of our fishermen by research and other methods. What is causing so much distress in the industry is the lack of markets and the loss of former markets. This has jeopardized our position in the traditional fish markets. Markets for Atlantic fish products must be recovered and new ones opened up if the industry is to survive.
The Miramichi fishing industry remains, on the whole, fairly steady. Catches of the different species of fish fluctuate, however, and the economy of fishing villages and of the Miramichi fishing industry has its ups and downs. Most of the products are in the delicacy class and a ready market is found for them. The problem is the lack of quantity, which makes conservation measures of prime importance for the future. Public attention was focused on the Miramichi area last year when lobster poachers became very aggressive and in one instance resorted to the use of firearms to scare off protection officers. Illegal fishing, and in particular tactics employed to scare off protection officers are condemned by the vast majority of fishermen who are law abiding citizens, who work the hardest for the smallest remuneration, and who realize that illegal fishing has serious effects on future stocks, a factor which subsequently affects the livelihood of all those engaged in the various phases of the industry.
On previous occasions I have requested the Department of Fisheries to provide a series of talks to fishing groups in their respective localities augmented by the showing of films, slides and charts in order to emphasize the importance of conservation and the drastic results of illegal fishing, and to impress upon fishermen the dangers of taking undersized fish, in particular fish that are necessary for propagation.
Although an educational program would bring about splendid results there will always be a few men who will fish illegally. It is necessary, therefore, to maintain active and progressive protection measures in order to protect the industry and safeguard the livelihood of law abiding fishermen. More aggressive measures should be taken against purchasers of illegal fish. If the outlets where illegal fish are sold are put out of business

The Address-Mr. Lahaye illegal fishing on a large scale will be eliminated, particularly in the lobster fishing industry.
A request has been made by the Miramichi salmon drifters association for a change in the drift net fishing season dates. The minister has informed me that the matter will be referred to the Atlantic salmon co-ordinating committee. Other representations have been made from time to time by the Miramichi commercial fishing association and the Miramichi salmon association incorporated. All aspects of Miramichi salmon fishing should receive exhaustive study by the co-ordinating committee before the committee makes its annual recommendations to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) with regard to bringing about mutual agreement on the fishing dates among the three groups, namely the drifters, the set netters and sport fishermen.
Fishing facilities on the Miramichi river are, on the whole, fairly adequate. There are, however, a number of small fishing areas which lack adequate facilities and I trust these will be provided in the near future.
Mr. Speaker, I will repeat what I have said on former occasions in this house: the status of the Department of Fisheries should be raised and additional moneys provided so that the department may do the things that are necessary to be done in order to bring the Atlantic fishing industry into its proper perspective so that it can fully promote the industry which is so vital to the economy of the Atlantic provinces.
In conclusion, I urge the government to put into effect now a plan of action designed to ease the recession and to bring back the stability of the Canadian dollar. Whatever action is required, drastic though it may be, the Canadian people look to this government to measure up to the task, while the people, for their part, are prepared to do whatever is necessary to safeguard the future of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is with mixed feelings of apprehension and pride that I accept the responsibility of speaking for the first time in the House of Commons.
Like those who spoke before me, may I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I admire the dignity and the competence with which you are conducting the proceedings of this house and which give them the sober character that becomes the highest chamber of this country.


May I congratulate also the deputy speaker (Mr. Sevigny) as well as the deputy chairman of committees of the whole (Mr. Rea).
I feel bound to refer to the last by-election which brought new members to this house. I congratulate those new members, particularly the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), who adds to this house a new note of brightness. On this point, I recall the particularly pleasant remark of one of my predecessors here, now president of the legislative council of the province of Quebec, the hon. Jean Louis Baribeau, who used to say that "an assembly without women, is like a garden without flowers", a statement I am pleased to endorse at this time.
I want to congratulate particularly the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Jorgenson). I listened to his speech very carefully, because he is a western farmer. Being a farmer myself, I was particularly interested. He said that western Canada faces a very serious problem, perhaps the most serious of all, that of wheat. I was glad to see that this year, the Conservative government has succeeded in exporting more wheat than ever before. This is a proof of the government's efficiency. I rejoice with the western farmer about that.
Nor did I fail to note, Mr. Speaker, that in the course of his remarks, the hon. member referred to problems which are similar to those of the eastern farmers. I take this opportunity to say that, for the first time, and in an efficient way, a government has shown concern for the eastern farmers of Canada. We had been used in the past to consider agriculture as a western business. I am glad that active consideration is being given to the benefit of the Canadian western farmers, but I am now much happier to note that the government now concerns itself with the problems of all Canadian farmers, both of western and eastern Canada.
May I merely mention, as evidence of that, the magnificent bill introduced last year, that is, the Agricultural Stabilization Act, which helped the eastern farmers-those small farmers still operating a family farm-to face the future with a little confidence and to stop being the victims of that uncertainty which had always been their lot under previous regimes.
As soon as the Conservative government came into power in 1957, I had the opportunity and pleasure of being part of the Quebec delegation which had come to meet those of the other provinces, and ask the

newly-elected government-in fact, it was so recently elected, at the time, that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) was still only acting minister-to do something to stop the dumping of poultry, and more particularly of turkeys, on the Canadian market. The situation was such that in the fall of 1956, Canadian producers had to sell at a loss on a dwindling market. I am happy to state that from then on, the Conservative government began to concern itself with the plight of Canadian poultry breeders and that, right away, we obtained from the ministers who met us on that occasion

I attended the meeting as the representative of the turkey breeders of the province of Quebec and also, if I may be allowed to mention this, as president of the biggest and best turkey hatchery in Quebec province, the Batiscan hatchery-as I was saying, we immediately obtained the establishment of a control over imports of turkey meat from the United States. As a matter of fact, I think it was the following day that a cabinet order settled the situation, with the following results: while we had imported 6,500,000 pounds of turkey and chicken meat from the United States in 1957, the figure for 1958, following establishment of this control and despite certain protests to the Minister of Agriculture, was only 167,000 pounds of old turkey meat suitable for soup, and about 300,000 pounds of roasting turkey. Those were the imports made up to last October.
This shows the difference, Mr. Speaker between the situation existing in 1957, when our imports reached 6J million pounds of turkey meat, and the situation in 1958, when the figure was kept down to about 500,000 pounds. Here is a case of action to improve agricultural conditions in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, to assess improvements that have occurred in the agricultural field, I think it can still be useful to review the situation previously obtaining. I shall not go back very far, but it is a historical fact that at the end of the Korean war, we, the farmers of the province of Quebec, felt at the time

that was in 1950-51-that our income could compare quite favourably with that of other classes of society. We then sold beef at 40 to 50 cents a pound, pork at about 50 cents a pound, and milk at $3.50 a hundredweight, which made the situation normal. Later on, agricultural conditions in the province kept deteriorating, reaching a period where milk sold at $2 and a few cents per hundred-weight. The price of pork fell to
The Address-Mr. Lahaye 22 or 23 cents a pound, which was the minimum price at the time, and beef fell as low as 20 cents a pound.
This drop in prices made the farmer's situation absolutely unbearable, and forced farmers' sons to leave home. These young farmers, the very life blood and future of our country, were moving to the cities.
Hog prices, at the time, fluctuated to an extent that I would describe as indecent, if I may be pardoned the phrase. Some farmers were buying hogs 4 to 5 weeks old, when prices were running between 35 and 40 cents, in the hope of selling them at the same price; but, when the time came to sell them, prices had dropped to 23 cents, with disastrous results for many of our breeders. Such was the situation facing our farmers when the government of the Right Hon. John Diefen-baker came to power. At present, the price of hogs is at a minimum, I'll grant you that. This is understandable, since hog breeding has developed in an extraordinary way in Canada. Therefore, we are glad that prices have remained stable and that the United States are there to absorb our surpluses in that field. The situation will probably remain the same with minimum prices, for we must necessarily face the situation as it is now. We are glad that prices remain reasonably fair, because at the present time the United States are still importing our surplus quantities.
With regard to an important point referred to the other day by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) when he spoke of what he called... vertical integration-I apologize for having hesitated over that word -I fully agree with his remarks.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the difficulties we are experiencing in the sale of pork, and which seem to be extending to poultry as well, are the result of the purchasing policies of certain firms, but mainly stem from the fact that certain firms dealing in feeds strongly insist that farmers get organized to practise what is termed speculative raising.
Mr. Speaker, I caution our farmers against this danger, and urge them to retain their independence. I would hate to see our agricultural class play into the hands of firms that are more concerned with their own interests than with the interests of our farmers. I urge our farmers to remain free, and should they decide to go into speculative raising, I remind them that this represents an initial

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take a few minutes of my maiden speech to speak briefly about my constituency. The constituency of Champlain, Mr. Speaker, bears an historical and symbolic name. Last summer, in Quebec city, we had the pleasure of celebrating the third centenary of the arrival of Samuel de Champlain and of the foundation of the city.
I wish to talk about Champlain constituency because the name of Champlain has not come up for many years. I will speak objectively, reasonably and fairly. Champlain constituency, Mr. Speaker, is on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, overlooking the city of Three Rivers and extending east. You will understand, Mr. Speaker, how proud I am to be located so close to the heart of the province of Quebec, and the outpourings of a generous heart necessarily overflow on the neighbour constituency.
The Champlain constituency takes up about 30 miles of the north shore of the St. Lawrence. It is a very promising place from an


industrial standpoint. I should like to give an obvious proof of this in saying that the city of Cap de la Madeleine, particularly well known to Catholics, because of its pilgrimage shrine, has nearly doubled its population in the last ten years and that new industries are being set up there constantly. I am convinced that, with transportation facilities, the quality of the soil-although I am not a geologist-and the advantage resulting from its proximity to the St. Lawrence river, that city is bound to develop rapidly and I think that before long some industries will move east to Champlain, Ba-tiscan and Ste. Anne de la Perade parishes, the latter being a large village already boasting of a few industries.
Though I am not much of a prophet, I expect that in the future, the constituency of Champlain will develop as a great industrial district. And I see no reason why the St. Lawrence, whose channel runs particularly close to the shores of my constituency, should not give rise to considerable development.
This is not to imply, by any means, that the constituency of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) will suffer from it. I also hope the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer), whose constituency of Three Rivers is next to mine, will not feel jealous because of developments taking place to the east. I think I am realistic enough to be allowed to touch upon these matters.
I foresee for the constituency of Champlain, where the deep water channel nearly touches the shore, the early development of all kinds of industries. Those lands cannot conceivably remain farm lands. I also think I can state- although this is somewhat more difficult- that soon winter navigation on the river will develop, and that, probably, the cities of Three Rivers and Cap de la Madeleine will become terminal harbours for winter navigation. Again, I say this without prejudice to the hon. members for the ridings situated below Three Rivers, as well as those from Montreal ridings.
However, I honestly believe it will always be hard, especially in the wintertime, as we can see this year, to cross Lake St. Pierre, a sea of still water, a widening of the St. Lawrence river, 20 miles wide, where there is no current. For this reason, I feel that even if the suggestion is disregarded regarding winter navigation as far as Montreal, except in a case like this year when severe cold has held up ocean-going vessels, it

would be easy in ordinary times to extend winter navigation as far as Three Rivers, which would result in further expansion.
This brings me to the present situation concerning navigation. I am familiar with this subject because many navigators come from my constituency of Champlain. There are some 500 navigators in my riding and certain problems are of special concern to them. In the first place, inland navigation, according to them, should be left specifically to our Canadian fleet. It is obvious that an ocean-going vessel can certainly carry a shipment as far as Fort William, Chicago and Milwaukee, in the United States, but in my opinion we should also control coastal shipping, inland navigation, so that it would remain in the hands of Canadian ships and Canadian companies. Maybe a lot will have to be done before applying this principle all down the line, but I believe an attempt should be made to carry it out.
There is also another situation I am particularly interested in. While I was reading the papers recently, an article caught my attention; perhaps it will be gratifying for my hon. friends opposite to hear that I read it in he Devoir of Saturday, January 24 last. It dealt with a protest made on behalf of pilots, with regard to a statement reportedly made at a meeting of the Dominion Marine Association and of the Lake Carriers Association of the United States, in Ottawa, when opposition was made to the compulsory payment of pilot fees to the Pilots Association of the Montreal and Quebec area, and it was suggested that almost anyone could do the job. I am quite familiar with the usefulness of this association, since many pilots in my small community belong to it. To become a pilot in the St. Lawrence river, a sailor has to go into apprenticeship for at least ten years, and then work many more years as an apprentice. Therefore he does not become a full-fledged pilot until he is almost thirty. In my opinion, such a training is necessary. As a matter of fact, if there is any important profession, it is that one, because pilots are responsible for a ship worth 3, 4 or 5 million dollars. I fail to see how the helm of a ship could safely be left in the hands of a man who never learned from experience how to steer a ship in a channel which is hardly more than a ditch, which a navigator has to know like he does the palm of his hand. I do not think any inexperienced person should be allowed to
The Address-Mr. Lahaye pilot a ship on the St. Lawrence, where there is danger not only for the ship itself but for the other ships it might meet. It is somewhat like the granting of a licence to a car driver. No licence is granted to a ten-year old child; but it will be to someone who has given evidence of his ability to drive. All the more care should be taken when a million dollar ship is at stake.
Allow me also to make a suggestion with regard to piloting between Montreal and Kingston. Some six or seven pilots in my constituency work in the Montreal-Kingston area, and they complain that they do not enjoy the same benefits as those enjoyed by the pilots of the St. Lawrence, from Montreal to Three Rivers and from Three Rivers to Quebec. I agree there is no obligation to employ licensed pilots. Most ocean-going vessels hire pilots, but there is no rule requiring ship owners to employ licensed pilots. I am aware of the particular difficulty involved due to the fact that part of the waterways is American. Besides from Cornwall to Kingston, arrangements would have to be made with the U.S. government in regard to those pilots. Just the same, it remains a fact that from Montreal up to the approaches to Cornwall, it should be easy to grant our pilots in that district the same status and the same guarantee as those enjoyed by the Montreal pilots. Therefore I would ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), a far-sighted man, to do all he can and give serious consideration to the problem.
Mr. Speaker, from the beginning of the session I have heard speakers of opposite parties making nebulous speeches and constantly chiding us claiming that the country was going down the drain. Allow me to say that had the opposition represented the situation more truthfully and realistically, we would not have been forced to make optimistic speeches in order to balance the picture. For two hours the Leader of the Opposition twisted the statistics and the reports in an effort to extract facts showing that under the present government, everything is going to pot. I realize that this is a method of practising politics, but to me it is definitely too one-sided. And I am most sincere in saying that such theatricals are apt to discredit him and to sow the seeds of uncertainty among the Canadian people. Fortunately, we are getting used to such pictures, and they make little impression. Still, there is quite a contrast

At that time, they would promise general and practically eternal prosperity, whereas today everything has changed overnight. Today, they show constant pessimism, an attitude that I think is dangerous and unhealthy.
Mr. Speaker, we hear statements from the opposition to the effect that this government has done nothing to relieve unemployment. Preposterous! I say to the hon. members of the opposition, what about the $500 million which were released to the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation in order to promote housing, to say nothing of the additional funds invested by loan companies as a result of this measure? Post offices are now under construction. It may look like quite ordinary things to you, but if I take a look at my riding,-I do not pretend to be a national administrator, even though I am that as a member of parliament,-I notice we have now a post office under construction. Construction in Cap de la Madeleine is substantial. We even notice a considerable increase over what it was last year.

Gentlemen of the opposition, instead of looking at things in this manner, instead of spending your time blackening the situation,- on purpose, I believe,-try to be reasonable. Give the true picture of the situation, stop looking for the worst, just for the sake of darkening the picture.
