Mr. Speaker, I want to tell the house that, since the beginning of this session, the hon. member for Roberval has been heckling, which shows that his political education could have been acquired only at the Duplessis school.
The Address-Mr. Boulanger
It is also the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), together with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fair-clough), who gave us a fancy footwork exhibition, which nobody had asked for, when they stated that O Canada was not our national anthem, but a pretty song. Those two ministers have displayed their narrowmindedness in thus riding rough-shod over the ideals of all right-thinking citizens of Canada. And they did the same thing to the Canadianism for which we have been fighting for so long. At the same time, they subjected all Conservative members to ridicule for none of them protested.
Mr. Speaker, it is equally strange to notice the courteous attitude taken by the government with regard to the settlement of the dispute which occurred between Canadian National employees and the management of that company. Everyone knows that the cabinet, even though the Prime Minister was away on his world tour, took the initiative of settling the question by promising an increase of 17 per cent in transportation rates, an increase which now affects the whole population and especially the farmers. The Prime Minister seems much more prone to settle commonwealth problems than those existing within this country. If he does not want to intervene, or if he does not authorize his ministers to act, so that the dispute may be settled favourably for both sides, they shall have to do so in a more humiliating fashion in the near future.
The people served by the C.B.C. French network are beginning to feel annoyed at paying taxes for a service which has already cost so much money.
Mr. Speaker, I will in the course of my speech, talk about another matter which is of concern to the population of Ontario and Quebec in particular, and more particularly to people in the province of Quebec: that of the textile industry.
I would have liked to deal with farm problems, but I believe that the problem of the textile industry is more important at this time. However, may I inform the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) that, time permitting, I will have a few words for him at the end of my speech. Last year, the house had quite a debate on textiles when the matter of tariff on imports of woollens and of the anti-dumping legislation came up. Unfortunately, being in hospital at the time, I could not take part in that debate.

The Address-Mr. Boulanger
At the time, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and several members on the government side went all out in their attempts to show that the slump in the textile industry of Canada was due to the Liberal party. The Minister of Finance had this to say. I quote from page 3470 of the Hansard:
I have stressed that this problem was not our creation. This was one more of the problems to which we have been heir when our predecessors- our do-nothing predecessors-went out of office. Surely the textile industry and the tens of thousands of Canadian workers in that industry are entitled to receive some intelligent understanding of their problems and some sympathy in the light of their difficulties.
And later, he said:
This industry deserves something more than words and it will require more than words to meet its needs.
We were all anxious to know the magic formula that the Minister of Finance would use to restore that industry to its original strength. This formula was a 2 per cent tariff increase on woollen goods, which means, in practice, an increase of 15 cents in the cost of woollen goods used in the manufacture of clothes, and an increase of about 25 cents in the cost of material used in the manufacture of an overcoat. These were the words the Minister of Finance used to indicate that the consumer would not be really affected by this increase and that the textile industry would be saved. He had just saved the country's textile industry; the workers would henceforth have jobs; gone would be the days of unemployment in the cities of the eastern townships, and in cities with textile plants.
How far can the Minister of Finance go to mislead the people, and to have them believe that he has done wonders for the textile industry?
The government has the same attitude as it had during the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958. We were told that the Conservative government, once in office, would settle the problem of the textile industry. The Minister of Finance himself came to Quebec to say that a vote for Conservative candidates was a vote for a solution to the problems of the textile industry.
The Prime Minister, at certain points, and in preparation of his election campaign wrote in 1957, in the textile industry manual, the following comments:
(Text):
It is a complete indication of what the industry's spokesmen have been saying tor a very long time and particularly in the past few years when you had special reason to ask for a better understanding of your needs and problems.

(Translation):
In the course of that debate last year, the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) quoted figures to prove that it was the fault of the Liberal government that the textile industry was in a slump. He added the following words, which I quote from the Hansard of August 13 1958, page 3467:
While in 1930, that industry was supplying 71 per cent of the national consumption, in 1957 it got only 57 per cent of the domestic market, always under a Liberal regime. From 1950 to 1955, still under a Liberal regime, foreign producers were allowed to grab 43 per cent of our national consumption.
I must say that the figures quoted by the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot are meaningless, having no direct bearing on the primary or secondary textile industry.
He closed his remarks by claiming to represent the textile workers of St. Hyacinthe in thanking the Minister of Finance for the position he had adopted towards the textile industry.
Another member from the Eastern Townships, the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), also expressed his thanks, and I quote his words as reported in the Hansard of August 12 1958, page 3443:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to item 554B, I thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for accepting the Tariff Board's recommendation for a slight increase in the rate of this item. I also very greatly appreciate his stating, in his budget speech of June 15 last, his intention to amend the definition of the term "dumping" so that the value of the price of foreign products shall include production costs, and a reasonable margin for sale costs, carrying charges and profit.
As the present discussion relates to the textile industry. I take this opportunity of commending the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) on adding 40 more assessors to the staff of various customs offices in this country.
Again it is the hon. member for Sherbrooke who said in the house, on May 16 1958, as recorded on pages 175 and 176 of Hansard:
On discovering so much uneasiness and unemployment in our textile industry we must expose the profound and remote causes. Nothing satisfactory was done by the former Liberal administration since 1935, either to adjust the customs tariff or to prohibit the import into Canada of foreign products which flood our markets and paralyse production in our own industry. More especially, during the past 10 years, the former Liberal administration has been giving free rein to foreign competitors and, in a blind and improvident manner, has left our Canadian market at the mercy and whim of imports coming in from Japan, the Indies, Italy, England, West Germany and the United States.
What has happened since the Conservatives came into power? Has the situation improved? No, Mr. Speaker, the situation is worse than ever. The number of people

employed has been steadily decreasing and the volume of importations has been greater than ever.
There are facts and figures which are more eloquent than some honourable members' fine words. Let me quote some of them in order to prove that this government did nothing to better the lot of the textile industry in Canada.
I refer to our cotton primary industry. If we look into the Cotton Institute of Canada report we find that, for the quarter ending June 30, 1958, the share left to our industries in the production of cotton fabrics for our Canadian requirements is 43 per cent. That is the lowest level ever reached by that industry. In 1957, that share was 46 per cent; in 1956, it was 51 per cent; in 1955, 54 per cent. If we were carrying our enquiry further, we would find that the share then left to our industry was even greater.
In the first eight months of 1958, American exports in Canada increased 225 per cent compared with the same period in 1957, in regard to drill, twill, sateen, broadcloth, twilled cotton material, etc.
In fact, between those two periods, our imports from the United States increased from 6 million yards for the first eight months of 1957 to 13,528,000 yards for the same period in 1958.
The amount of imported materials during the last eight months is therefore much higher than during the twelve months of previous years.
The main reason, although not the only one, is the sharp increase of imported American materials on our Canadian markets, the entry into Canada of a great quantity of first quality American products that are passed as second quality products.
An investigation conducted among Canadian manufacturers who use the materials mentioned above, in the manufacture of garments, has shown that 50 per cent of the fabrics used in 1958 were imported into this country as substandard products thus enjoying the discount provided by the act, a discount reaching as high as 10 per cent, depending on the class.
I emphasize especially that the United States, to promote their sales on foreign markets, pay a premium to American mills which ship manufactured cotton goods to Canada on the basis of the raw cotton content of the product. The premium is approximately six cents a pound. The premium thus paid by the American government is a definitely unfair practice detrimental to our Canadian producers. It is a particular
The Address-Mr. Boulanger incentive for Americans who thus make more profit on their sales, or lower prices when competition gets too tough.
Other tactics sometimes used to a certain extent by American manufacturers consist in deliberately placing a piece of fabric of a different colour into a bale of some first quality material, thus contributing to lower its class and price, or in intentionally cutting a yardage into pieces of various lengths, acceptable to the buyer, thus making possible their classification into a lower category, and even including first quality pieces in the same shipment bearing the second quality label, always for the purpose of securing a lower excise tax rate or customs tariff.
Those practices are detrimental to our industry and to our trade; they are slowly destroying what is left of factories in this country and forcing Canadian workers into unemployment.
I read in a report of the Cotton Institute some comments which aptly describe the present situation:
It is difficult to understand why Canada was required in 1957 to accept 67 per cent of all bedspreads exported by the United States, 64 per cent of all cotton towels, 78 per cent of all cotton drapes and draperies, and 34 per cent of sheets and pillow covers.
The most tragic aspect of the situation is the fact that American exports to Canada are ruining the Canadian textile industries to the benefit of the United States factories, however insignificant and negligible such advantage may be to them. The 218 million yards of cotton cloth which the United States exported into Canada last year represent 77 per cent of the Canadian production, but only 2.5 per cent of the United States production. In other words, if the United States had not exported cotton cloth to Canada last year, the American factories would have lost only two hours a week, and Canadian factories could have increased their production by 75 per cent and paid $45 million more in wages and salaries to Canadian workers. If imports from the United States had been cut down by half, this would have meant a loss of only an hour a week in the United States cotton factories, but $22 million more in wages and salaries for these Canadians.
The 22 million yards of processed drills, twills and cotton satin which will have entered Canada at the end of that year (1958) will have practically ruined this market for Canadian factories, but represent only 2\ per cent of the 981 million yards of goods of these categories, produced in the United States.

Our imports of any textile product except hats, was $8,812,000 in 1957 and for the first eight months of 1958 our imports had increased to $9,186,795. All told, Mr. Speaker, the textile industry as a whole has reached its lowest level of activity ever recorded. Certain segments of the industry have already folded up under the pressure, and others will follow suit if adequate action is not taken to ensure the industry's survival.
The manufacturers-we can say this in fairness to them-have done their part to improve equipment and production methods so as to compete with other countries.
Workers have waived salary increases so that employers might hold out and keep the plants in operation. In fact, comparing average earnings of textile workers with earnings in various other trades requiring similar training and qualifications, it is found that an assembler in one of our automobile plants earns $1.94 an hour; an electrician, $2.24; whereas a weaver in the textile industry earns $1.36, and a carding machine operator, $1.24 per hour.
Neither the workers, who have endured great sacrifices, nor the employers, who have

kept abreast of technical progress, are to blame for the dilemma with which the textile industry is faced. The matter of its survival now rests with the government, as was stated by Mr. H. Dobbie, president of the Woollen and Knit Goods Manufacturers Association. Another expert, Mr. Roy Crabtree, president of the Basic Textile Institute, recently stated that "the industry has done just about everything possible to help develop its own protection against this tremendous competition" from countries with low production costs. The industry must now look to the government to take remedial action.
This is what the mayors of Sherbrooke, Granby, Cowansville, Three Rivers, St. Hya-cinthe, Richmond and Princeville are asking in the petitions sent by Mr. Marcel Marier, mayor of Drummondville, to the Prime Minister on February 11, 1958, and on January 12 of this year. It is also the request of the Eastern Townships Textile Association, sent by its president, Mr. J. S. Moynan, and its 130 directors and technicians, and the request also of the Chambers of Commerce of the region as well as other Eastern Townships organizations. These requests made by the population of the region I represent here are merely a consequence of the glittering promises made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to go on, but I am told that my time is up. May I say in conclusion that the confusion in which the government finds itself becomes increasingly intolerable for the public in general, and especially for those who are interested in the textile industry. If the government does not renounce this policy of confusion and announce a more definite one as soon as possible, in this regard, I intend to come back on that matter at each opportunity that I will have during this session to remind him of the fine promises he made to the industry for the sole purpose of having its term of office renewed.

Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to speak for a few minutes about my own constituency of Essex West. The rural areas of Essex county are generally speaking about equally apportioned between the constituencies of Essex South and Essex East. Until the last election no Conservative had been elected in Essex West since 1930.
Statistics are usually boring and uninteresting and for that reason I shall not unduly burden the house, but there is much about the city of Windsor and its environs that is not generally known and certainly not fully appreciated. The latest statistics I have available were compiled by the Windsor chamber of commerce as at August 1 last. I shall at this point refer rather extensively to the data thus acquired. Windsor is Canada's largest city on the United States-Canada border and situated on the busiest waterway in the world. During the 1957 season, a period of 282 days, vessel passages in both directions upon this water totalled 20,642 or 73 vessels per day, or one vessel every 20 minutes, carrying a total of over 130 million tons of cargo on this waterway. There were ships of great length, as long as 729 feet, carrying iron ore, coal and grain through this great inland water route of the great lakes system.

It is a geographical coincidence that in Windsor we are south of the United States and between Detroit and Windsor there cross in both directions each year over 17 million persons, close to 5 million of whom are United States visitors to Canada. The metropolitan population of Detroit alone is 3,670,000. Windsor is one of Canada's great industrial communities, manufacturing a wide variety of products in 475 industries. Only four cities in Canada produce more than Windsor. Windsor's selling value, according to statistics of the dominion bureau of statistics, in one year was $474,634,000.
During the past year there has been a monthly average of 36,148 employed in Windsor industries. While Windsor is well known for automobile manufacturing, and I mention the products of Chrysler Motor Corporation, engines and parts of the Ford Motor Corporation and engines for General Motors Corporation, it produces many other products such as a wide range of pharmaceutical and other nationally advertised products, one of which I may mention, namely Walker's Canadian Club, an industry of which we are very proud and which provides year-around employment for many, many people in our city.
According to official estimates for 1958, Windsor is also fifth in Canada, according to volume, in capital investment in new industrial construction, machinery and equipment. The figure for one year, 1958, was $30.1 million. An annual average of 1,282 new homes have been built in Windsor during the past four years. The area is also well served by five main railroads and one terminal line, the trans-Canada network airlines and adequate highway transportation facilities.
Windsor, too, is determined to realize every advantage of the St. Lawrence deep waterway after it is built, which now provides great lakes transportation. With all recent improvements costing $9.37 million, Windsor has the second lowest per capita gross debenture debt in Ontario, according to the latest available statistics. Windsor has completed the construction of a municipal courts building and has started plans for development of over 1,200 feet of river-front property in the downtown area where there will be initially erected a civic auditorium and a convention hall. The Hiram Walker historical museum was opened on the site on May 7, 1958. Now completed is the new city


hall to be fronted by an esplanade extending to Riverside drive. We also have the best facilities for education and a university, Assumption university of Windsor, with Essex, Holy Redeemer, Holy Name, Canterbury and University colleges as affiliates.
Perhaps I should also say something about the county of Essex. Windsor and Essex county, together having a population of 246,000, enjoy the news services of an outstanding Canadian newspaper, the Windsor Star with a circulation of over 78,000, ten weekly newspapers, radio stations CBE, CJSP and CKLW, and television station CKLW-TV, the most powerful television station on the North American continent, with an approved rating of 325,000 watts.
Windsor's industry is well balanced with a prosperous agricultural community well known as the sun parlour of Canada where 33 different fruit and vegetable crops are produced. Because of the favourable climate, with an average winter high of 35 degrees and a low of 27 degrees, an average summer high of 78 degrees and a low of 58 degrees, and a long growing season averaging 171 days, the county produces fruits and vegetables which reach market one to five weeks earlier than any other area in Canada. The farms of Essex county have a higher per capita production than anywhere else in Canada.
I should like to make some particular observations with regard to our industrial workers. A survey made by the Battelle memorial institute on the economic development opportunities of Windsor reveals that no Canadian metropolitan area is as dependent upon the manufacture of one type of commodity for its well-being as is Windsor upon the automotive industry. Consequently when economic factors adversely affect this important industry the people of Windsor suffer in direct proportion thereto. Furthermore, when government fiscal policies place a further handicap upon the industry by way of a special excise tax, insult is added to injury and our people suffer to an unjust and disproportionate extent. That is why we in Windsor over the years have appealed to the Liberal government of the day time and time again but without marked success to remove what must be recognized by all fair minded people as a rankly discriminatory tax against one segment of our economy.
I shall return te this topic later but the point I want to make at the moment is that one of our greatest assets in the greater

Windsor area is our industrial workers. In the past as in the present we have had in the area a heavy concentration of industry and because of that, we have a manpower pool of workers and technicians possessing mechanical skills and talents to a greater extent, relatively speaking, than anywhere else in Canada. They are, taken at large and despite some beliefs to the contrary in some quarters, fine, intelligent well-informed and conscientious citizens, and I am proud of them. It is true that our people are perhaps more unionized than in other communities. It is also true that our union leadership leaves much to be desired. Our municipal authorities in years past have also contributed to much of our industrial strife. But those are all things of the past. We have today a healthy industrial climate and, generally speaking, good labour-management relations. In 1957 there were no man days lost in Windsor's automotive industry due to strikes.
Another point I should like to make is that our workers do not submit to dictation or domination by their political leaders. I think perhaps that is general across the country. The Windsor political action committee, which professes to speak for labour and endeavours to control and direct its voting, has over the years endorsed the candidates of the C.C.F. party. On occasions in the past it has had a measure of success. In the last two federal general elections in 1957 and 1958 an intense and concerted effort was made to swing Windsor labour to the support of the C.C.F. party. They concentrated their efforts upon Essex West possibly because there appeared to be little hope of defeating the deeply entrenched hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who had been given in 1953 one of the largest majorities in Canada.
They selected a well-known formidable candidate and experienced campaigner, he having been a city alderman, and undoubtedly the strongest candidate they could find. What were the results? In 1957 he secured almost 22 per cent of the vote and running again in 1958 secured only 19 per cent and made the usual contribution to the country's exchequer. No, labour by and large supported the Conservative party and I agree with an observation to that effect made by the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Campbell) during the last session. But, Mr. Speaker, I must be excused for correcting his statement that in the last election labour in Windsor supported the Liberals. I would not be here today were it not otherwise.
Let us take a look at what happened in neighbouring Essex East. The hon. member

I should like now to return to the excise tax on automobiles. This tax was originally imposed as a wartime expedient, and I do not quarrel with that. However, there is no basis for its retention in peacetime. It has not been completely removed since the last war, and it should never have been increased by the Liberal government in 1947 to 25 per cent. On March 23, 1949, it was reduced to 10 per cent, and the record since then is as follows: On September 8, 1950, it was increased to 15 per cent; on April 11, 1951, it was further increased to 25 per cent; on April 9, 1952, it was reduced to 15 per cent; on April 6, 1955, it was further reduced to 10 per cent. On December 7, 1957, the Conservative government under our esteemed Prime Minister further reduced the tax by one-quarter to 7 per cent. I congratulate the government upon this action, and I urge the Prime Minister and his colleagues to give favourable consideration to a further reduction and the eventual elimination of this tax at the earliest possible date compatible with the needs of the economy.
The hon. member for Essex East, and the former member for Essex West failed dismally

The Address-Mr. Spencer to sufficiently espouse the cause of their constituents, while they were supporters of the Liberal government, to see to it that this discriminatory tax was removed at a time when additional tax revenue was no longer required for government operations.
A few months hence a period of daylight saving time and confusion will begin. Some municipalities will adopt daylight saving time while others will refuse. Some areas will move their clocks forward at one time, and others at another. Some will return to standard time later than others. A traveller will never be sure until he arrives at his destination and sees a clock whether he is an hour ahead of time or on time or an hour late for his appointment, or whether the places of business are open or closed. This could be quite disconcerting if, after a long day's drive, the vendor dispensing liquid refreshments should be closed. All in all, it is so confusing and needless.
During the war we quickly ended this nonsense. We decided that daylight was worth saving. A federal regulation switched the whole country over and back again simultaneously. There was a minimum of confusion, and no one seriously complained. Why should it not be done again? Surely there can be a happy medium struck between the conflicting time changes and an end to this annual muddle and perplexing state of confusion. I urge the government to give serious consideration to the removal of this annoying and unnecessary period of uncertainty.
I should like now, in the few minutes at my disposal, to speak very briefly of the unemployment situation in general and that pertaining in Windsor in particular. The favourite theme of the Liberal party has been unemployment and from the speeches and comments of the opposition, particularly those of the hon. member for Essex East, one would conclude that unemployment is a tragedy which only descended on us in the last year or two since the present government took office. Of course, this is just plain nonsense. It would be ludicrous if it were not for the fact that we on this side of the house are genuinely disturbed about the ill effects of the economic recession, and the government has shown its concern by taking effective action to alleviate the situation. I am not going to review the measures taken by the government as I would be repeating what has been said in this house and, in any event, they are well known.
What I want to stress, however, is that we had a serious unemployment problem before the present government took office. I have before me a report on unemployment as recorded in the Windsor office of the unemployment insurance commission since the

beginning of 1953. Without going into details, the record certainly reveals a need for action to stimulate the economy. I have made a search, and I can find nowhere the advocacy by the hon. member for Essex East in this house, while he was a member of the government, of the elimination of the excise tax on automobiles in order to stimulate the sale of automobiles throughout the country and thus create jobs for our unemployed in the city of Windsor. The then member for Essex West was obviously aware of the situation because I found recorded an inquiry of the minister of labour as to whether anything could be done to rectify the serious unemployment in Windsor. This was on February 7, 1957, at a time when it was becoming embarrassing in view of the expected general election.
What remedy did the government provide for our people? Sometime in May an announcement was made that the moving expenses of our unemployed would be paid by the government if they could secure employment elsewhere. This was the cure for our ills prescribed by the former minister of labour.
In conclusion, I should like to contrast that record of indifference and neglect of the mounting unemployed rolls with the record of the present government. There was an immediate appreciation of the gravity of the economic doldrums into which the former government had allowed us to drift and a program of remedial measures was initiated and since pursued with vigour, the beneficial effects of which are now revealed in the upswing which has begun. The people of Canada made a wise decision when they turned out the former government before conditions became irremedial, because under the leadership of this government and our Prime Minister we can go forward with confidence and optimism toward a more prosperous and still greater destiny.

I support his motion of non-confidence concerning the way the affairs of this country have been administered by the Conservative government for the last 19 months. What has been the result of that administration? There are 750,000 people looking for jobs, which means that about 3 million of our fellow citizens are living in worry, misery and discouragement in a country of 17 million inhabitants. Nearly 18 per cent of our population, if we take into account only those who are unemployed at this moment, are in a sad plight indeed. How many more will be added to this number from now to next May?
Inflation has affected at least 6 million individuals with fixed revenue, that is pensioners, small wage earners, small merchants and farmers. These people are discouraged and lack the necessary money to buy the bare necessities. There is at present a slump in business from one end of the country to the other, and when we refer to those facts we are branded as defeatists.
What have you done, my friends of the Conservative government, since 1957? You have spent the surplus, $350 million that the Liberal party had accumulated in 1956 and 1957. You have shown a deficit of $50 million for the administration of 1957 and 1958. Furthermore, you have spent about $300,000 belonging to the unemployment insurance fund; you have shown a deficit of several million dollars for old age pensions, and probably a deficit of a billion dollars for the administration of 1958-1959. This is not too bad! What good administrators you are! The country was in full prosperity when you took power, when everything was going fine. In fact, the situation had never been so good, with the exception of the slackening of business which always occurs during the few months preceding a general election. It is not extraordinary for our country; this slowing down lasted only a few months, but in the United States it is felt for three or four months before each general election. Compare yourselves to us, Liberals, who had to take charge of the administration of the country in 1935. At that time most Canadians were in bankruptcy. It took but five years of a Conservative administration, from 1930 to 1935, to plunge the country into debt and to take it to the brink of bankruptcy. We will soon find ourselves in the same economic difficulties if, by mischance, you stay in power for five years. The situation will get worse. This is what happened between 1931 and 1935, as I just said, and I should know because I was in business then. Two thirds of our
The Address-Mr. Gour farmers were under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act or were going to be so placed; otherwise, they would have lost their farms. Three out of five general stores in my village of Casselman went bankrupt and their owners lost all their personal property. I survived, but not without struggle and hardship. I was mayor of my town from 1931 to 1934; three quarters of the people were on relief; across the whole country, thousands of municipalities were bankrupt and under trusteeship of provincial governments. Mr. Speaker, my first remarks must, of course, be ones of congratulation to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and to the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I know, sir, that there have been many remarks made already in this chamber congratulating those two hon. gentlemen and it would be simple enough for me to agree in principle with what has been said. I think, too, that the press of Canada has perhaps paid the greatest compliment to them-a compliment far greater than any individual member of the house could convey-by describing their remarks in this chamber as setting the keynote for this debate, something which has not been done in many years.
I took a great deal of interest, in particular, in the remarks made by the mover of the address when he gave his very mature appreciation of the problems of agriculture. He not only did that, but, without emotion, he described the history of the industry and explained how we find ourselves in our present situation. He recommended, as one would


expect from an hon. member on this side, some constructive suggestions to the government and accordingly his stature in this house improved with each syllable he uttered. As I walked out of the chamber and listened to the comments being made I was particularly impressed by some words by a member of the protective staff who had been listening. He said this was the first speech on agriculture that he had ever understood. And as I watched the leading exponent on this topic, that great agricultural expert, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), I gathered that he found himself in the same category as the gentleman who made that observation.
I should like, also, to compliment the seconder of the address because all too often do we hear people in our country, whether in parliament, in this chamber or outside, speak of national unity as something which we can accept without working for it. I propose in the latter part of what I have to say, not to offer a suggestion to the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet but, rather, to take up his challenge, because the keynote of his address was to me the fact that the area which he represents has given the lead to each and every province to make certain that we accept the challenge of national unity such as he has described.
The nature of this debate finds me in practically the same batting order as I was a year ago. I have no intention of labouring unduly the weakness of the opposition. However, I will not resist the temptation to draw to the attention of this house one rather interesting aspect-that on every occasion on which we have seen the opposition speak or engage in any conversation over C.B.C. television stations we have seen no indication of this desire to come out fighting which we have heard so much about. I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, with regard to this group of gentlemen who wanted to come out fighting that after the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) had torn their arguments apart piece by piece their front bench members began to slip slowly further down in their seats until all we could see of them was the heels of their shoes before the Prime Minister was through.
I do not intend to say any more about the contribution they may or may not have made to the debate, but I should like to say a word about the television performance of the hon. member for Essex East, because at that particular time he was asked a number of questions about what he would do in the event he ever found himself again in government. On each occasion he replied that not having all the facts in front of him he was

The Address-Mr. A. R. Smith
not able to come to a firm conclusion. I remember, in particular, a question asked by Mr. Charles Lynch with regard to his opinion on the recognition of communist China. The nimble piece of footwork performed by the hon. member would have done credit to the best ballerina in the country; he literally danced off the stage before he made any reply at all.
And now, if I may, I should like to turn my attention to a matter of more serious and, I hope, of a more consequential nature. I am sure all of us were delighted that Canada today is participating in discussions on an international basis with the United States. I refer to the Canada-United States joint committee. I was very happy to hear the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) tell us of the part he had played in this. I congratulate him on his contribution to this debate, because it was a most important one. We in the city of Calgary enjoy a relationship with the United States which is very unusual and it is perhaps significant in this respect that in our consular area we have more than 60,000 United States citizens, the greatest concentration of Americans outside the United States itself. We have enjoyed a relationship which is an example to the rest of the world. These United States citizens are not just welcome transients but men and women who have made a contribution to the business, industrial and social life of our city. I think we have set an example to the rest of the world in being able to get along with our neighbours.
I do not think any of us would disagree that with regard to diplomatic problems-* and perhaps I should say not so much diplomatic as economic problems-there has been some erosion of our relationship with our great neighbour to the south. But it would be equally wrong for us to suggest that the problems we have before us are insurmountable, and the important part of this committee's work has already been established in so far as it is going to be asked to define where the area of disagreement actually lies. We will, in effect, separate fact from fiction; we will determine what the problem is and attempt, as members of two legislative bodies, to resolve it, bringing recommendations back to our respective governments in the hope that some action can be taken to reconcile the differences which are before us. I suggest that the most important advance we have already made lies in the fact that this committee has been established.
I congratulate this government, which has been alleged in the past to have been antiAmerican, upon taking the first step toward some constructive action to improve our relationship with our fine friends south of
the border. The difficulty with regard to our relationship with the United States lies, in so far as we have been concerned, in the fact that we have at times felt ourselves to be neglected-maybe misunderstood is the better word. I suggest that the action taken by the United States congress and by its speaker gives a clear indication that they recognize the problem.
I wish to call the attention of the house to four particularly important actions taken on their part. The first, of course, was by the President of the United States coming here to discuss mutual problems in this very chamber. The second was when the United States congress extended the reciprocal trade act. The third was when Mr. Brook Hays and Mr. Frank Coffin presented their report, and the fourth was when the President, on the suggestion of the Prime Minister, appointed the United States counterpart of the Canadian committee. This is a very clear indication that the United States realizes that our difficulties can only be surmounted by a frank understanding as to where the problem actually exists.
I believe that the committee can accomplish a great deal. It is not an instrument that will become a debating society because the two countries recognize that the differences are economic. My hope is that the citizens of both Canada and the United States will stop shooting verbal rockets at one another based on differences and issues that do not really exist, but rather that having defined the area of their disagreement they will like mature men and women resolve their differences. I suggest that this can also be done at the legislative level.
Perhaps if I were to say a word about defence it might be construed that having had the privilege of serving as chairman on the committee on estimates last year, which committee examined the estimates of the Department of National Defence, I am setting myself up as an authority on the subject. This is most certainly not the case. But having made reference to the estimates committee may I be permitted to take advantage of this my first opportunity to do so and to thank, first of all, the committee members for making our work all the more agreeable. Through their co-operation we were able to complete our work in very short order.
I should like to extend to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) the sincere appreciation of the committee for the time he gave to us. Whenever he attended meetings of the committee he answered in detail all the questions that were put to him, and he made himself available at all times. I

The Address-Mr. A. R. Smith also wish to say to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) that their co-operation was greatly appreciated.
Having made reference to the work of that committee may I perhaps suggest that hon. members of that committee had full opportunity last year to discuss the question of defence in minute detail and I feel it would serve very little purpose to attempt to go back and review any of that discussion in this session of parliament in the light of any change in the international situation or the defence picture for we must realize the restricted nature of any new developments.
But what is our defence picture? In the past year we have seen introduced in this house what I suggest is a rather narrow form of nationalism on the part of a few hon. gentlemen who have indicated a resistance toward any suggestions for the integration of Canada's defence forces with those of the United States in any form of defence alliance and particularly through the NORAD agreement. Surely it is time we set aside this question of having our rights infringed upon when mutual defence is in the interest of our national survival. We must realize that national defence is not something one can arrange to suit one's own convenience and there must be cognizance of national and international needs. There can be no question of this house not having been given every opportunity to debate the question of joint defence. The most important aspect of this matter is that we are conducting our defence on a co-operative basis and thus are providing protection not just for either country but for the continent as a whole.
Perhaps the most important aspect of defence this year is the recognition that we are in a transitional period. For example, with respect to manned aircraft, whether it be the CF-100, the Sabre or the CF-105, they have a life expectancy that cannot be calculated beyond a few years. We also know that missile warfare is something that will soon be upon us if it is not already. Let us recognize that this is a transitional period and bear in mind that in expending monies for defence we must do so with one eye on the present and one eye on the future. It is ridiculous for us to expend large sums of money on the development of any piece of military equipment which in only a few months will be obsolete and of no value to the defence of the country as a whole.
I am, however, one of those who believe there is a period in the foreseeable future when a manned interceptor may be required to meet the 1,500 to 1,700 existing manned bombers of a potential enemy. Until this

situation changes it is unthinkable that we should put ourselves in a position where we could not defend ourselves on that basis. I do not intend to enter into the argument about the relative merits of the CF-105, the United States CF-106 or the F-108 that will not be off the production line for some four years, but as one who has flown in defence of our country I believe we must maintain a flexible defence policy involving the flexibility of military equipment. Any aircraft we adopt should be capable of being related to our missile program but not dependent on it.
About missiles themselves, we know they are weapons that can be employed with great accuracy but of course they have shortcomings. While it is important to think in terms of defending ourselves on the home front we must also consider the commitments we have under the NATO agreement which will require additional types of weapons.
I have brought to the attention of hon. members matters that are perhaps already only too familiar to the Department of National Defence, but before leaving the subject I should like to say a few words about home defence. There has been no conflict whatsoever on the part of the government in any statement it has made and particularly concerning whether or not we will likely require a first-class two seat interceptor. Every statement that has been made by this government clearly indicates the need for a combination of weapons and every statement that was made in the committee on estimates when it examined the estimates of the Department of National Defence supports this position. What I want to make clear is this: last year the government spent $174 million for a one year extension of the Arrow program, and at that time had flown only four of the CF-105's. Certainly the government is not going to accept or reject this particular aircraft until it is fully acquainted with its flight characteristics.
Recognizing that we are passing through a transitional period in defence, it does not make sense to say that we must evolve a hard and fast rule concerning what type of weapon or group of weapons we are going to employ until we know what the qualifications of those weapons are. The government must have the full facts at hand before making a decision, and it will test and review various types of equipment in order to decide on their suitability to fit into the pattern of international defence under the NORAD agreement. Then and only then can a decision be made. No attempt on the part of hon. members of the opposition and particularly on the part of the Leader of the Opposition, who on many occasions in the past few days has expressed

some doubt about the acceptability of the Arrow, is going to force this government into a premature and untimely decision.
Before leaving the subject of defence may I make a second suggestion that applies to the defence of our country. Our commitments under NATO are gradually disappearing. Many of the responsibilities we have will be relinquished. Some of the airfields we have in Canada will doubtless be abandoned. I would suggest to the Minister of National Defence that in co-operation with the Department of Transport consideration should be given to the question of how these airfields can best be utilized.
In my own city, for example, we have an airfield, formerly the No. 3 service flying unit, which will become surplus at some point. Canada has a growing civil aviation problem and to some extent private, commercial and executive aircraft are cluttering up the principal airfields in our cities. I think it is time we recognized that we should transfer our civil aircraft to those subsidiary fields which are about or nearly about to be declared surplus. If we did that we would accomplish two things. First of all, we would have alternate air fields near our cities for defence purposes in the future. But what is more important, we would be providing incentive for civilian aviation to develop to a greater extent than it has in the past without in any way complicating commercial air routing.
While I am on the same subject I should like to suggest the advantage of giving some thought to permitting our auxiliary squadrons to have an additional role, namely that of carrying out air search and rescue in many areas of our country not adequately covered today. For the most part auxiliary squadrons have been transferred to air transport command where they use twin engine expediter aircraft. They are comparable to any of the light bombers which were used in the early stage of the war. I think the squadrons would be more effective in providing more help in search and rescue, which to some extent has been neglected in many sections of Canada.
I come now to a subject which perhaps has been introduced in this chamber before and about which I have seen a rather interesting change. I refer to the amount of lobbying which exists in parliament today. I refer to lobbying by outside interests which in itself is in no way offensive. In fact, I did some research and drew a parallel with some pressure groups, or lobbying of legislation, in the United States. It is not unlike our own country some 25 or 40 years ago. I recognize the constitutional difference between our parliament and the United States congress. In
The Address-Mr. A. R. Smith the United States, because of the constitutional differences lobbying can have a great deal more effect than it has here, but what I would point out is that in the United States as early as 1867 there was a group of gentlemen who decided that lobbying had reached such proportions as to become extreme. The first attempt at a bill was introduced at that time. Some years later the bill on lobbying was introduced and only as recently as 1946 did we see any legislation which had any teeth in it.
I do not for a moment, Mr. Speaker, deny the right of individuals either in a body or as a group to approach any member of parliament on any business with which they may be concerned. Because of the very nature of our constitutional right here we make ourselves accessible to anyone within Canada who has a problem. But I suggest that the history of pressure groups and lobbying in the United States is not unlike our own in this respect. These groups, because of their size, because of their operation and because of their effectiveness in obtaining the legislative result they required eventually were asked to file with the United States administration two facts, namely their source of income and their affiliation with the people with whom they were doing business.
I think that at some time we may be forced into the position of referring to a committee of this house whatever information we can to determine whether lobbying has become so effective in Canada today that similar legislation to that passed by the United States is required here, namely legislation having to do with the registration of lobbyists. I am not speaking mainly of those who may wish to make a phone call and describe a problem to a member. I am not referring to those who may wish to make an appointment and present a problem to an individual. I am referring to that vast army of people who descend on the capital. They may describe themselves as public relations men or even members of the press. They have been known to be members of that very important profession, the legal profession. I am not confusing those of the legal profession who are here set up as agents to do business on behalf of companies, but rather to that group on the outside who know that legislation may be introduced at this session or at some future session and who think they should be here to make absolutely certain that the greatest and most effective pressure can be brought to bear on every member of this chamber.
It is quite possible that we may not have reached the day when legislation is required. I realize, too, that any legislation that may be introduced would not necessarily be the whole answer to the problem because in

The Address-Mr. A. R. Smith the United States since 1946 some 2,800 lobbies have been registered which operate within the law. What I do suggest is that it is a regulation which, if it is not required at present, may at some time in the future be of great help to the individual member, not that hon. members need to be protected. I would not be so naive as to suggest that an hon. member is not familiar with the subject that may be discussed with him, but only that he should have the opportunity of discerning the particular objective required in the lobby which is undertaken at that time. As I said initially in introducing this matter I do not suggest that there should not be any information given nor do I deny the individual the right to be given the opportunity to carry out whatever undertaking he has in mind.
I am going to close the remarks I have made tonight with a reference to the oil and gas industry and it will be brief. Shortly there will be introduced in this chamber legislation having to do with an energy board, something that has been long required in the history of the petroleum and natural gas industry. We assume that the legislation will involve on the one hand the interests of the consumer and on the other hand provide some help to the industry which it will govern. I will not at this point make any reference to it but I would like simply to introduce a note of optimism at this time which is the first time I have had the opportunity of speaking on oil and gas in the past two years. The marketing of our petroleum products has taken the first encouraging upturn that we have seen in the past two and one-half years. This has been due largely to the expansion of the Ontario market which has more than doubled itself in the past two years.
The most significant aspect of the Ontario improvement has been the desire on the part of the industry itself to divert portions of crude which at one time were taken from foreign sources. In addition, crude was forced back which had been coming in from Montreal refineries, thus limiting again foreign imports into the country. I think too it can be said that the hope for a future market in the United States has improved, again because on the one hand General Petroleum Corporation and their refinery at Ferndale in Washington state have replaced foreign crude with Canadian crude from western Canada which was also under their control.
The point I make, is that the industry for the most part has corrected to a very large degree its own problem. I think it is to be congratulated first of all on recognizing that that problem is best left in the hands of the


industry itself, with the minimum amount of control or regulation. I do not for a moment suggest that there is not going to be a demand or a desire for the eventual construction of a pipe line to the Montreal area. In my opinion it is only a matter of time before that will take place. The marketing picture will improve which will clearly indicate that the market demand has taken up some of the slack of the overproduction which we have had in western Canada. But in the long term our ability to produce will, as it does today, far exceed our ability to sell oil. Therefore it is essential, not only from the point of view of the economic picture in Canada but in the interests of national defence, eventually to move oil into the Ontario and Montreal refining area.
Second, I would say this. Our hope of moving more oil into Montreal or of increasing the market in Ontario is in my view at present second only to the necessity of improving market export into the Pacific northwest and the great lakes area of the United States. In any event, it can be said that for this year, certainly for the first two months of the new year, the market picture for export and for domestic demand has increased beyond all expectations. In fact, in the first two months of this year we are only a little below the record year in 1957 during the Suez crisis.
I think if anything is to be said about oil and gas we have to comment on two other aspects. First of all, there is the fact that the Venezuelan government has seen fit to increase taxation on the companies operating in that country. This could have a very interesting effect because it will inevitably bring about an increased price for Venezuelan crude which must move into foreign markets. It would be wrong for me to suggest that these oil companies or, for that matter, the government will attempt to outprice themselves completely so far as foreign markets are concerned, but it is significant to note that any suggestion of further concessions by these producers, either in Canada or the United States, which in the past has made it impossible for Canadian crude to compete will be certainly short lived if not completely eliminated. I hope that the market for Canadian crude, both in the Pacific northwest and also in Ontario and Montreal, is broadened considerably, first of all by the more efficient manner in which we produce oil and, second, because of the change in the international situation as it affects Venezuela.
Finally, so far as oil and gas industry is concerned, there will be introduced into the house more oil and gas legislation than at any time in the whole history of the Canadian parliament. I suggest this is going to

be something with which each and every member must concern himself because this is Canada's No. 1 mineral industry, one which today has grown to maturity, which affects not just the four areas in which the product is produced but which has an influence on every province in our Canadian economy. Therefore it is my hope that hon. members will not only look into the recommendations contained in the Borden report but will examine the areas where this industry affects the particular economy of their own constituencies.
Speaking as a member of parliament I say that we need the greatest help from every section of the community to put together the best recommendations which can be introduced into legislation. We also know that there are going to be many new and interesting events which will affect the industry. A few of us had the opportunity today, for example, to view, certainly for the first time in some years, an experiment which conceivably may be carried out in the very rich Athabasca tar sands. This area, as is well known to the House of Commons, contains the greatest known reserve of oil. The experiment which was demonstrated to us through a motion picture will be carried out by the Richfield Oil Corporation as a possible answer to the separation of the oil from the sand, thus making available in some future year this great source of crude oil.
There are, of course, a great number of others who are interested in this prospect, but what it amounts to is that the year 1959, with the improvement in the domestic oil picture, with the opportunity that may exist in future demands from United States sources and in view of the eventual construction of pipe lines, improvement in oil and gas policies both on the provincial and federal level and the effect of more important improvements in the technological field, will unquestionably be the industry's greatest year.
As I close my discussion of oil perhaps I should say that I know that very shortly the petroleum and natural gas conservation board will make available its decision on whether or not to recommend a permit for export. This is something which will be in the hands of the federal government to consider, and I know I speak on behalf of my constituents when I say for them that I hope the government will give the earliest consideration to this matter. I say this because, assuming that an export permit is considered and recognizing that the Borden commission and the petroleum and natural gas conservation board have both suggested that we have gas reserves far beyond domestic requirements for Canadian consumption, I think it can be
The Address-Mr. Pearson said that the export of our surplus requirements is a most beneficial thing so far as the Canadian economy is concerned.
I close on the theme introduced by the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne when he discussed in such eloquent terms the need for national unity. I think he will agree with me, as I am sure every other hon. member of the house will, that while national unity is something that is present today we have achieved a measure of economic unity which permits each province, each section of each constituency for that matter, to be able to be a part of the family of confederation and feel that they are not poor relations because if you understand where your problems exist and survive that is what creates national unity. I believe and I am sure that the majority of the people of our country believe that if we have any portion of national unity, as the hon. member suggests, and I agree with him, certainly we have attained it because of our achievements in economic unity and equality which include the construction of the railroad, the improvement in the farm population's rather difficult situation of a year ago, the improvement of the position of the maritime provinces, the improvement of the picture in British Columbia today, all of which have been part and parcel of the operations of Conservative government. That is the reason we enjoy national unity today, because this is the government that has made it possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the closing moments of the discussion of the subamendment to state the position of this party in respect thereto. Before doing so, I should like to say that I have listened with great interest to the interesting and, I thought, on the whole constructive contribution made to the debate by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. He mentioned among other things the desirability of proceeding carefully and not making premature decisions in regard to such an important matter as the CF-105. I would remind him, if a reminder is necessary, that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) told us in the committee over which he presided with such efficiency last session that the decision in this matter would be made in the autumn, last autumn. Certainly the statement of the government on that matter in September did not constitute that decision which we had been led to expect would have been made at that time. If a decision has to be made, and we on this side appreciate the difficulties of that decision, perhaps it would have been better if it had been made last autumn and before March 31.

The Address-Mr. Pearson
The hon. member also expressed some suspicion about the development of what he called lobbies, and suggested, as I understood him, that the time might be coming when we would have to register those who could be called lobbyists, as is done at the present time in the United States. I hope, Mr. Speaker, we will not have to consider any such procedure as this when it comes to the right of Canadians, individually or collectively, to make their views known to the government of the day. We remember in that connection the statements that were made not very long ago that the doors of the government would always be open, I hope not only to those who are registered for that purpose.
We on this side had hoped that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), in that intervention which he made with his usual vigour and forcefulness a week ago today, would have given us and the country a considered and constructive analysis of the economic and other problems which face the country now, and the principles on which the government proposes to act through legislation in meeting those problems. The Prime Minister, on that occasion at least, did not give us that kind of statement. He criticized me for taking an unduly gloomy and pessimistic view of the situation. He said that I spoke irresponsibly and in a way-I hope I am not misinterpreting what he said-which was not consistent with the danger which we faced at this time from communism. Communism, Mr. Speaker, had nothing to do with what I was talking about on that occasion. I suggest that we do not assist the fight against communism abroad by not dealing effectively and immediately and constructively with the problems that we face at home. I do not believe it was in accordance with what I said to interpret my remarks, as the Prime Minister did on page 52 of Hansard for January 19, 1959, as painting a picture of Canada as a place, fearful in its prospects and frightening in its future.
There is only one thing which can prevent Canada from achieving the destiny which is hers if her people desire to achieve it, and that is the loss of peace and world war III, which will prevent any country from achieving any destiny in this world. Inadequate policies of government can postpone, and I suggest if we do not get the right policies from the present government we may postpone the achievement of that destiny, but no Canadian, whatever party he belongs to, lacks faith in the achievement by Canada of the destiny which is hers and the realization of the national vision which we all have before us.


The Prime Minister also thought that we were exaggerating the economic and financial difficulties that face us. I made certain specific statements and colleagues of mine followed them up with other specific statements which we attempted to support by the official statistics which were available to us. We gave certain concrete evidence in support of those statements, and I do not feel the Prime Minister or his colleagues in government have dealt effectively, and as we had reason to believe they would, with the points of criticism which we advanced. I asked certain questions of the government which are recorded on page 41 of Hansard for January 19, 1959, very definite questions. They were meant to be constructive questions. They were meant to elicit from the Prime Minister and the government the principles upon which they were going to act in the introduction of their legislation. These questions have not been mentioned, let alone replied to by any spokesman for the government since this debate began.
I also made three additional concrete, and I thought constructive suggestions concerning other matters and how we should proceed in regard to them. They also have not been referred to by any speaker on the government side in this debate. I wish I had the time to put those questions which appear on page 41 on the record again, but they are there.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) made an interesting intervention in the debate which included very little indeed about the policies of his government, but a good deal about the policies and personalities, particularly this personality, of the preceding government. He told us once again with some satisfaction how the commonwealth had been saved by a government which had always believed in the commonwealth from a party which had never believed in the commonwealth. Once again he has not produced the evidence to support that kind of wrong statement. I refer the minister, not to his own words but to his own actions. I refer him to his trade diversion policy which has resulted in exports from the commonwealth to the United States being increased by 15 per cent, as I pointed out the other day, and exports from the commonwealth to Canada being decreased. I refer him to the free trade offer made by the British government a year or so ago, about which nothing has been done. I refer him to the increase in wool duty. It is a homely old saying, Mr. Speaker, but it remains true, that actions still speak a good deal louder than words, even the words of my hon. friends.

My hon. friend also said with some satisfaction that he and his government had saved us from the United States. He expressed his preference for jackboot over tiptoe diplomacy in relation to that country. He did a great deal of threshing of old straw, but once again we can let the record speak for itself. Perhaps it would have been more useful if we had at this time from the minister some indication of the trade policies of this government, some views on the proposals that have been made on this side concerning the restoration of the Hyde Park agreement; some indication of the attitude of the government toward economic and trade developments in Europe which will have, if they develop in a certain way, a far-reaching effect indeed on the trade of Canada as well as on the trade of the United States.
Mr. Speaker, we have before us the subamendment moved by the C.C.F. One part of that subamendment refers to the government in agricultural and anti-inflationary policies, which of course we can unreservedly support. We could have found even more examples, but we thought it wise to concentrate, by exclusive mention, on unemployment, which is such a pressing and immediate problem in human and social as well as economic terms. There is another part of the C.C.F. subamendment. A reference to the absence of social and economic planning which calls for approval of a socialist approach or a socialist solution for national problems would make it impossible for us to support such an amendment to the address.
On this occasion, however, Mr. Speaker, and this is in contrast to previous occasions when these words were used, we have noted a reference specifically to the confused policies of the government which were criticized by us, among other reasons, precisely because they were unplanned and were carried out in a piecemeal, hit-and-miss, short-sighted fashion. We agree that there is not the kind of economic planning which is both desirable and necessary to meet these problems which are before us today. Because we feel that that kind of planning is essential for this particular purpose, we shall be able to support and vote for the C.C.F. subamendment.
